Overview of Malaria Epidemiology, Control and Policy Gaps Malaria is a major public health issue in Africa, leading to widespread illness and fatalities, especially among vulnerable populations such as under five age children and pregnant women [ 1 ]. It is caused by the Plasmodium parasite, transmitted by infected Anopheles mosquitoes that thrive in warm, humid environments. The disease is prevalent across sub‐Saharan Africa, with East Africa facing a disproportionate impact due to varied ecological conditions, socioeconomic factors, and inconsistent healthcare infrastructure [ 2 ]. The WHO's 2023 World Malaria Report estimates 263 million cases and 597,000 deaths globally, an increase of 11 million cases from 2022. About 95% of deaths occurred in the African Region, where many at‐risk individuals lack access to essential services [ 3 ]. In Ethiopia malaria remains the top public health challenge with 7.3 million cases and 1157 deaths reported between January and October 2024 [ 4 ]. Approximately 75% of the country is malaria‐endemic, putting 69% of the population at risk. For instance, evidence shows that under‐five‐aged children, periodic outbreaks contribute to up to 20% of deaths. This reflects poor case management and control strategies, and defects in drug use policies [ 4 ]. The report of 2025 showed that malaria incidence remains highest in Uganda, South Sudan, and Burundi, greater than 250 per 1000, while Eritrea and Comoros report the lowest rates [ 5 ]. Artemisinin partial resistance has surpassed 20% in several regions. Pyrethroid resistance in Anopheles mosquitoes, climate change, and small funding are jeopardising the prevailing malaria challenges in the region [ 5 ]. According to the 2022 report, there are marked differences in malaria incidence and mortality rates across East Africa. Burundi, South Sudan, and Uganda shoulder relatively the highest incidence of over 250 cases per 1000 population, with correspondingly high mortality [ 6 ]. The lowest incidence rates are reported in Eritrea and Comoros. And Kenya, Ethiopia, and Somalia account for moderate incidence levels (Figure 1 ). The reported regional disparities point to the need for tailored, country‐specific malaria control strategies as well as comprehensive surveillance. FIGURE 1 Preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta‐analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram of the study inclusion process. For instance, in Ethiopia, the primary vector control strategies for malaria elimination include the use of long‐lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS) [ 7 ]. These interventions effectively reduce the risk of malaria infection by targeting indoor‐biting mosquitoes. However, while LLINs and IRS have proven effective in controlling malaria transmission, they alone are not sufficient to achieve malaria elimination [ 7 ]. But the country national malaria strategic plan (NMSP), which spans from 2021/22–2025/26 aims to consolidate the gains made so far, sustain and expand impacts. The programme's vision is to see a malaria‐free Ethiopia. Tanzania also adopted ACTs as first‐line treatment. The study examined the process of priority‐setting for selection of first‐line Artemether‐lumefantrine using the accountability for reasonableness framework and found that, while evidence was used, stakeholder involvement and transparency were limited [ 8 ]. Evidence noted there are challenges of implementing ACT policy in contexts with complex health systems, conflict zones, and weak infrastructure. For several decades, many malaria‐endemic countries relied on chloroquine to treat Plasmodium falciparum malaria [ 9 ]. Widespread resistance has drastically diminished its efficacy, prompting the subsequent adoption of amodiaquine monotherapy and sulfadoxine‐pyrimethamine [ 10 ]. ATC now recommended by the World Health Organization and supported by the global fund for uncomplicated falciparum malaria are Artemisinin‐based combination treatments (ACT); these are combinations of an Artemisinin derivative and another structurally unrelated and more slowly eliminated antimalarial. WHO has also ‘raised the bar’ recently in recommending that cure rates should be at least 90% and preferably > 95%, assessed at ≥ 28 days [ 11 ]. Despite these efforts, resistance continues to escalate, with Artemisinin and partner‐drug resistance now threatening malaria control in high‐burden areas [ 12 ]. A recent molecular epidemiology study conducted in Ethiopia revealed that the k13 R622I mutation was the most prevalent, appearing in 15.7% of samples with notable regional variation. Importantly, three validated Artemisinin‐resistance (ART‐R) mutations P441L, P574L, and A675V were identified in Ethiopia for the first time, with A675V detected exclusively in a Gambella clinic serving refugees from Sudan and South Sudan. Furthermore, polymorphisms associated with partner drug resistance including those in the crt , mdr1 , dhps , and dhfr genes were found to be nearly fixed. The majority of samples (87.2%) contained monogenomic infections (COI = 1), and mutant parasites exhibited high local genetic relatedness at the health facility level, suggesting clonal transmission. Principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated distinct regional clustering, particularly in Gambella, underscoring the roles of local drug pressure, regional transmission dynamics, and cross‐border importation in shaping the observed resistance patterns [ 13 ]. The study also noted the first time A675V was found exclusively in a Gambella clinic serving refugees from Sudan and South Sudan [ 13 ]. The World Health Organization (WHO) summary lists Ethiopia and Sudan as suspected for Artemisinin partial resistance, although not yet fully confirmed by therapeutic efficacy studies across the board [ 14 ]. Evidence from Eritrea indicates that the day‐3 positive rate rising from 0.4% in 2016 to 4.2% in 2019 after ACT treatment, crossing the WHO threshold for declaring resistance [ 15 ]. The study also indicated a notable increase in the prevalence of the Pfkelch13 R622I mutation, which was detected in 109 of 818 isolates collected before treatment. Its frequency rose from 8.6% (24 of 278) in 2016 to 21.0% (69 of 329) in 2019, suggesting a concerning upward trend over time [ 15 ]. Artemisinin partial resistance (ArR) in Plasmodium falciparum has been associated with specific mutations in the pfkelch13 (K13) propeller domain across East Africa. Notably, the R561H mutation has been reported in Rwanda, Uganda, and Tanzania, representing a validated marker of partial resistance to Artemisinin‐based therapies [ 16 , 17 , 18 ]. In addition, the C469Y and A675V mutations have been detected in Uganda, where they are considered emerging or candidate markers linked to delayed parasite clearance. The presence of these mutations highlights the ongoing risk of Artemisinin resistance spreading in the region and underscores the importance of continuous molecular surveillance to inform treatment policies and containment strategies [ 17 , 18 ]. Additionally, in Rwanda, the presence of the pfkelch13 R561H mutation was associated with delayed parasite clearance, signalling the start of Artemisinin resistance [ 19 ]. The emergence of antimalarial drugs including ACT resistance may be associated with the presence of substandard formulations containing low amounts of active ingredients [ 20 ]. According to the Wellcome Trust, falsified or poor‐quality antimalarial drugs with little or no active ingredient can contribute to the development and spread of resistance. The circulation of substandard and falsified medicines further undermines treatment efforts, diminishing the efficacy of antimalarials including ACTs and compounding issues such as poor accessibility, inappropriate prescribing practices, and patient non‐adherence [ 21 ]. Additionally, subtherapeutic concentrations of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) in these poor‐quality medicines likely accelerated [ 22 , 23 ]. A 2019 review found substandard antimalarials as high as 88.4% in Africa and sub‐Saharan Africa shows that 35% of samples failed chemical analysis, emphasising the need for a multifaceted approach to control the production of substandard or falsified antimalarials [ 24 ]. Reports from Southeast Asia and Sub‐Saharan Africa reveal a significant burden of poor‐quality antimalarial drugs. In Southeast Asia, 35% of 1437 drug samples failed chemical analysis, 46% of 919 failed packaging analysis, and 36% of 1260 were identified as falsified. Similarly, in Sub‐Saharan Africa, 35% of 2297 samples failed chemical analysis, 36% of 77 failed packaging analysis, and 20% of 389 were classified as falsified [ 20 ]. Consequently, the growing prevalence of substandard and falsified antimalarials may constitute a serious yet underappreciated public health crisis, particularly in resource‐limited settings. The combination of poor‐quality antimalarial medicines and emerging drug resistance is a major threat to malaria control and elimination. Several reported cases of presumed antimalarial drug resistance have been subsequently attributed to substandard medication quality rather than genuine parasite resistance mechanisms [ 25 , 26 ]. The circulation of poor‐quality ACTs would facilitate the emergence and spread of Artemisinin‐resistant malaria parasites [ 21 ]. These issues, combined with socio‐economic barriers and weak healthcare infrastructure, jeopardise recent progress and demand coordinated, multifaceted responses to safeguard public health and advance toward malaria elimination goals in the African region, especially the eastern countries [ 27 , 28 ]. Additionally, the emergence of poor quality and resistance may contribute significantly to treatment failures [ 29 ]. In Ethiopia, surveillance reports and therapeutic efficacy studies (TES) have documented a treatment failure rate of about 1.9% among patients treated with artemether–lumefantrine (AL) for uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria [ 30 ]. The report from Rwanda also indicated that the prevalence of treatment failure rate as a result of triple therapy leads to resistance. The authors highlight an urgent need for policy interventions in Africa to curb the spread of Artemisinin‐resistant malaria and prevent widespread treatment failures [ 19 ]. Therefore, this study examines the dual challenges of substandard and falsified Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) and the emergence of Artemisinin resistance in East Africa, aiming to provide strategies that preserve effective malaria treatment and control in the region. 2. What is Known? Malaria remains one of the most significant public health challenges in Africa, particularly in East Africa where transmission is intense and disproportionately affects under‐five age children and pregnant women [ 1 ]. Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) have been the cornerstone of malaria treatment since their adoption as first‐line therapy in 2006 by the World Health Organization (WHO) [ 11 ]. However, the emergence of antimalarial drug resistance, poor regulatory oversight, and the circulation of substandard and falsified medicines have threatened recent gains in malaria control. Evidence shows that up to 35% of ACTs in sub‐Saharan Africa fail quality tests, while sporadic reports of treatment failure and molecular markers of Artemisinin resistance have raised serious concerns for long‐term malaria chemotherapeutic intervention in the management and elimination of malaria [ 24 ]. 3. What This Review Adds? This systematic review synthesises evidence from East Africa on the dual threats of poor‐quality ACTs and emerging Artemisinin resistance. It highlights country‐specific variations in ACT quality, ranging from no failures in Kenya (2018) to 42% failure rates in Ethiopia (2024), and persistent quality concerns in Uganda. Importantly, while clinical efficacy of ACTs remains high (≥ 90% PCR‐corrected cure rates), molecular surveillance has revealed early signs of resistance mutations, particularly k13 polymorphisms in Ethiopia and Uganda. The findings clearly point to a collaborative and comprehensive approach to further investigate the situation on the ground in all countries regarding substandard medicines and drug resistance. It also underlines the urgent need for harmonised regulatory systems and sustainable policy interventions to safeguard ACT efficacy and ensure progress toward malaria elimination goals in East Africa. 4. Rationale for the Review This systematic review aims to provide evidenced information on the magnitude of the circulation of substandard and falsified Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) in selected East African countries and presents key drivers contributing to the prevalence. It also identifies the molecular markers of Artemisinin resistance and evaluates the effectiveness of current regulatory frameworks in combating substandard and falsified antimalarial medicines. Moreover, it assesses the implications of poor quality medicines and emerging resistance on malaria treatment outcomes. Finally, the review formulates strategies that can be implemented to mitigate these challenges and strengthen the fight against malaria in East Africa. 5. Review Objectives This review aimed to achieve four main objectives: (1) to determine the prevalence of substandard and falsified Artemisinin‐based Combination Therapies (ACTs) in selected East African countries; (2) to assess the reported efficacy and safety profiles of ACTs in the region; (3) to evaluate the regulatory performance, clinical implications, and emerging challenges in addressing substandard and falsified antimalarial medicines; and (4) to propose policy strategies that ensure the availability of quality ACTs for effective malaria control and prevention. 6. Methodology 6.1. Search Strategy This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines, to enhance transparency by clearly reporting the rationale for the review, the methods employed, and the key findings [ 31 ]. The PRISMA checklist is presented in Table S1 . The study protocol was developed and registered in PROSPERO under number CRD420251135109 [ 32 ]. The review was conducted from 30‐July to 30‐September 2025. To ensure a comprehensive literature review, an extensive search was conducted across electronic databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar. The search focused on peer‐reviewed journal articles, national reports on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) related to Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs), evidence on substandard and falsified ACTs, regulatory information, and grey literature. A combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free‐text keywords was employed, with queries adapted for each database. Key search terms included: (‘Antimicrobial resistance’ OR ‘antimalarial resistance’) AND (‘East Africa’ OR ‘Ethiopia’ OR ‘Uganda’ OR ‘Kenya’ OR ‘Tanzania’ OR ‘Rwanda’) AND/OR (‘Counterfeit’ OR ‘fake’ OR ‘falsified’ OR ‘substandard’) AND (‘drug’ OR ‘medicine’ OR ‘pharmaceutical’ OR ‘antimalarial’ OR ‘Artemisinin‐based combination therapies’ OR ‘Artemether and Lumefantrine’ OR ‘Coartem’) AND (‘national medicine regulation’ OR ‘drug regulation’ OR ‘medicine regulatory’). Search strategies were refined using database‐specific filters, including publication year, language, and article type, to ensure relevance and comprehensiveness. 6.2. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Studies and reports were included in the review if they met specific criteria. Eligible study types encompassed narrative reviews, observational studies, systematic reviews, meta‐analyses, policy reports, national surveillance data, and intervention studies. In terms of relevance, included studies focused on malaria resistance to Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) and the prevalence of substandard or falsified ACTs in one or more East African countries, or provided comparative insights from similar low‐resource settings. Studies were excluded if they examined malaria resistance to ACTs solely within the context of environmental microbiology without direct implications for human health, or if they addressed substandard and falsified antimalarials without specifying prevalence related to ACTs. Additionally, opinion pieces, editorials, and letters lacking supporting empirical data from credible sources, and studies not offering specific insights relevant to East African countries were excluded. The inclusion criteria were defined based on the PICOS framework, which is discussed below [ 33 ]: Participants / Population : Patients with uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, including children under five, pregnant women, and adults in East African countries (Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Sudan). Also includes drug samples (ACTs) collected for quality evaluation (e.g., assays, dissolution, API content). Intervention : Use of Artemisinin‐Based Combination Therapies (ACTs) as first‐line treatment for uncomplicated malaria. Regimens studied include Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL), Artesunate‐amodiaquine (ASAQ), Artesunate‐mefloquin (ASMQ), Dihydroartemisinin‐piperaquine (DHA‐PPQ), and Artesunate‐sulfadoxine‐pyrimethamine (AS + SP) Comparator / Control : Comparator arms in clinical trials: Other ACTs (e.g., AL vs. ASAQ, DHA‐PPQ vs. AL). For quality studies: comparison of ACT samples against pharmacopoeia standards (assay, dissolution, impurity limits) Outcomes ( Main Outcomes ): Clinical Outcomes: PCR‐corrected Adequate Clinical and Parasitological Response (ACPR) at day 28, parasite and fever clearance rates, and adverse drug reactions (safety outcomes). Additionally, quality outcomes: Proportion of ACT samples failing quality control tests (assay, dissolution, API content, packaging compliance). Also, resistance outcomes: Presence of molecular markers of resistance (e.g., k13 polymorphisms, gene amplification, delayed parasite clearance) and regulatory/Policy Outcomes: Strength and effectiveness of national regulatory frameworks (post‐market surveillance, adherence to WHO guidelines, enforcement). Study characteristics : Designs included randomised controlled trials, therapeutic efficacy studies, observational surveys, molecular surveillance, Pharmacopoeia quality testing, systematic reviews, policy reports. Geographic scope: East African countries (Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Sudan). Time frame: Studies conducted between 2003 and 2025. Sample size: 45,769 patients in clinical efficacy studies and 40 eligible publications included in the qualitative systematic review. 6.3. Assessment of Methodological Study Quality The methodological quality of the published articles was assessed using the Medicine Quality Assessment Reporting Guidelines (MEDQUARG) to evaluate the quality of the methodology section [ 34 ], while the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) checklist [ 35 ] was applied to assess the clinical concerns related to Artemisinin‐based combination therapies. This systematic review applied the 12 core elements of the MEDQUARG medicine quality evaluation criteria (Table 1 ). Only studies that scored between 50% and 100% were included in the qualitative analysis, ensuring methodological rigour. Among the 10 studies assessed, four fulfilled all 12 criteria and achieved a score of 100%, while the remaining six scored between 83% and 91.7%. Although some of these studies reported only three of the core elements, the majority were consistent with MEDQUARG standards and were therefore included in the review. The quality study included study conducted based on WHO sampling strategies and drug monograph. Additionally, the modified STROBE checklist was applied to assess the quality and transparency of each observational study included in the review, covering 20 essential items related to antimalarial efficacy and regulatory performance (File S1 ). For inclusion in this study, all articles were required to be published in indexed journals accessible through PubMed and retrievable via Google Scholar. Reporting Bias, and Certainty Assessment In this systematic review, the risk of bias due to missing results was not assessed. Similarly, the certainty of findings was not evaluated, as this study is qualitative in nature. Instead, we focused on assessing the methodological quality of the included articles using a predefined checklist to ensure the validity of the review. 6.5. Data Extraction Two independent authors (YTM and AAT) conducted the screening and data extraction using predefined inclusion criteria. The process involved four steps: (1) Title and Abstract Screening, where studies were initially assessed for relevance; (2) Full‐Text Review, in which selected studies were examined in detail to confirm eligibility; (3) Data Extraction, using a structured form to systematically collect key information, including study design and objectives, prevalence and patterns of resistance to Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs), incidence of substandard and falsified ACTs, existing regulatory frameworks addressing these issues, implications for public health and emerging resistance, and strategies for mitigation; and (4) Discrepancy Resolution, whereby any disagreements between authors were resolved through discussion to reach consensus. 6.6. Data Synthesis, and Statistical Presentation The collected articles were imported into the Zotero reference manager. Data synthesis employed a narrative approach to summarise the key findings across the studies. Tables, figures, and descriptive narratives were used to present the data. Reported frequencies and percentages from the included articles were also considered. The analysis focused on identifying and examining themes and patterns related to the challenges associated with Artemisinin‐based Combination Therapies (ACTs), as well as the prevalence of substandard and falsified ACTs within the healthcare context of East African countries. 6.7. Review Context Definition 6.7.1. Substandard and Falsified Artemisinin‐Based Combination Therapies (SF‐ACTs) Antimalarial medicines that do not conform to the quality standards set by recognised pharmacopoeias (e.g., USP, BP) or fail to meet the specifications of their approved product registrations due to either poor manufacturing, degradation, or deliberate falsification. 6.7.2. Clinical Efficacy of ACTs The proportion of patients achieving adequate clinical and parasitological response, defined as the absence of parasitaemia on day 28 (or day 42 for long half‐life ACTs), without fulfilling any criteria for early or late treatment failure. 6.7.3. Regulatory Performance The capacity and effectiveness of National Medicines Regulatory Authorities (NMRAs) in East Africa to ensure that only quality‐assured antimalarials are registered, monitored, and made available in the market. 6.7.4. Emerging Concern The increasing threat of antimalarial drug resistance, particularly reduced susceptibility of Plasmodium falciparum to Artemisinin and partner drugs, compromises therapeutic effectiveness and public health outcomes. 6.7.5. East African Countries For the purpose of this study, it refers specifically to Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, and Rwanda. 7. Results, and Discussion A total of 6816 articles were identified through database searches. After title and abstract screening, 5389 records were excluded. The remaining 1427 articles underwent a full‐text review, of which 1387 were excluded due to study area mismatch, inadequate information, or being non‐empirical publications (e.g., opinion pieces, editorials). Ultimately, 40 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the qualitative systematic review (Figure 1 ). 7.1. Evolving Quality Landscape of Artemisinin‐Based Combination Therapies This systematic review examined the quality of Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) in Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and Rwanda (Table 1 ), revealing substantial variation across countries. In Ethiopia, studies spanning more than a decade show mixed findings: while no failures were reported in 2011 and 2014, later surveys highlighted emerging concerns. A 2019 study identified a 4% failure rate in lumefantrine products due to excessive active pharmaceutical ingredient (API), and the most recent 2024 investigation reported markedly higher failure rates of 42% for artemether and 12.5% for lumefantrine primarily linked to dissolution failures. Kenya and Tanzania also exhibited fluctuating trends. Kenya's earliest survey in 2004 revealed an alarming 50% failure rate, yet subsequent assessments showed steady progress, with no failures reported in 2018. In contrast, Tanzania's performance has been less consistent: although the WHO reported no failures in 2011, later studies recorded 12.1% (2015) and 61% (2024) failure rates, the latter largely attributed to incomplete product information rather than pharmacopoeia non‐compliance. Uganda stands out for its persistently high failure rates, with 36% of samples failing in 2010 and a multi‐country survey confirming that 22% of Ugandan ACTs did not meet quality standards. A total of 3363 ACT samples were tested across four East African countries, of which 375 samples failed at least one quality control test, corresponding to an overall failure rate of 11.2% (375/3363). The failure rate for each country was calculated based on the number of samples tested in that specific country, rather than using aggregated data from the region. As shown in Table 1 , Uganda reported the highest country‐specific failure rate at 33.3% (16/48), followed by Kenya at 14.1% (10/71), Tanzania at 11.6% (333/2859), and Ethiopia at 4.2% (16/385). The relatively high quality failure was reported in Tanzania (88.8%) followed by Ethiopia (4.3%), Uganda (4.3%), and Kenya (2.7%) (Table 2 ). The failure rate represents the proportion of failed samples relative to the total tested in each country, while the contribution reflects the share of total failed samples. Overall, 11.2% of ACT samples tested across these four countries did not meet the required quality specifications. It is evidenced that an estimated 122,350 (interquartile range [IQR]: 91,577–154,736) malaria‐related deaths among children under five were linked to the consumption of substandard or falsified antimalarials. This accounts for 3.75% (IQR: 2.81%–4.75%) of all under‐five deaths across 39 countries in Africa [ 36 ]. Poor‐quality antimalarial drugs, particularly Artemisinin‐based combinations, could also contribute to the development of drug resistance and worsen the growing drug resistance of Plasmodium falciparum to Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (40), which in turn could undermine malaria control and treatment efforts [ 37 ]. Thus, there needs to be strategic intervention in minimising the Artemisinin monotherapies as it is one of the contributing factors for resistance [ 38 ] and pronouncing the critical importance of pairing Artemisinin with an effective partner drug to prevent the emergence and spread of resistance [ 38 ]. 7.2. Failure Rate by Study Design, and Sampling Technique The review discussed the failure rate of ACT based on study design and sampling techniques (Table 3 ). The cross‐sectional surveys relying on purposive sampling, field visits or formal sector assessments (such as WHO‐supported surveys) generally reported very low or no failure rate (0%–8.3%). These methods tend to target registered outlets and therefore may underestimate the presence of poor quality ACT's in the wider market. In contrast, covert approaches such as mystery shopping and random sampling, which are more likely to capture informal or unregulated outlets, revealed substantially higher failure rate including 12%–36% in some surveys and up to 50% in small random‐sample study. This indicates how the sampling frame critically influences observed prevalence, with overt surveys reflecting formal supply chains, and covert/random approaches detecting hidden risks in less‐regulated markets [ 34 ]. Previous studies have also suggested that differences in study design and sampling techniques may account for discrepancies in the reported prevalence of poor‐quality drugs across studies and geographic regions [ 49 ]. factor is the definition of failure applied. While most studies assessed laboratory quality parameters such as assay, dissolution, and content uniformity, others focused on regulatory criteria such as labelling and product information compliance. For instance, one large cross‐sectional review of 1534 samples reported 61% failure, but this was limited to deficiency in laboratory‐based failure rates. This design‐dependent variability underlines the importance of aligning sampling strategies and outcome definitions when interpreting ACT quality data. According to Ozawa et al., failures in quality control parameters varied across studies. Among 9724 medication samples from 99 studies reporting API levels, 25.9% (95% CI: 19.3%–32.6%) contained less than 80% of the labelled API. Other issues included substandard API above 80%, disintegration, dissolution, degradation, impurities, or visual defects. Notably, 13.8% (95% CI: 9.0%–18.6%) of failed samples had less than 50% API, while 12.5% (95% CI: 7.8%–17.3%) contained either no API or the wrong API [ 50 ]. Hence, identifying sources of quality control parameters is critical. The presence of problems in the regulatory system, such as the absence of any pharmacopoeia belonging to any African country and variation/inconsistency in each country's regulatory set‐up, was indicated [ 51 ]. To effectively address such quality challenges, adopting a Quality by Design (QbD) approach within the quality assurance system can be highly beneficial, even under prevailing financial constraints [ 51 ]. Apart from regulatory implementation, manufacturers should exercise robust oversight during production to ensure that all raw materials are sourced authentically from authorised suppliers [ 52 ]. This vigilance not only safeguards product quality but also reinforces compliance with established standards and regulations. The existence of poor‐quality ACT in the region could contribute to economical wastage, treatment failure, and resistance. Evidence indicates little is known about the adverse health and economic impacts of substandard and falsified medicines (SFMs) in low‐ and middle‐income countries [ 53 ]. A systematic review conducted in 2023 revealed substandard and falsified antimalarial medicines can account for 10% to 40% of total annual malaria costs, and SFMs affect rural and poor populations disproportionately [ 53 ]. Substandard and falsified antimalarial medications place substantial health, social, and economic burdens on individuals and communities. Poor‐quality drugs could lead to treatment failures, prolong illness, and lead to unnecessary costs. In addition, these ineffective medicines can increase the length of hospital stays and death [ 54 , 55 ]. Evidence from Nigeria indicates that poor‐quality antimalarial medicines are responsible for approximately 12,300 deaths and USD 892 million in economic losses annually. These products also contribute to antimalarial drug resistance, which could increase the total economic burden by an additional USD 839 million (11%) [ 56 ]. The burden is particularly severe in the northern regions of Nigeria, which experience an estimated 9700 deaths and USD 698 million in total economic losses due to SFMs, antimalarials significantly higher than the burden observed in southern regions [ 56 ]. Additionally, an agent‐based model assessing the impact of substandard and falsified (SF) antimalarials in Uganda highlighted the substantial economic and health burden associated with poor‐quality antimalarial drugs [ 57 ]. According to a study conducted by Ozawa et al. from Uganda, malaria remains a major economic and health burden among children under 5 years of age, with an estimated annual impact of 614 million USD. The study found that for children who sought medical care, costs reached 403 million USD, of which 57.7 million USD were direct medical expenses [ 57 ]. A notable portion of this burden is driven by substandard and falsified antimalarials, contributing 31 million USD and responsible for 9% of malaria‐related deaths among care‐seeking children. Moreover, the scenario analysis suggests that widespread Artemisinin resistance could exacerbate this burden significantly, leading to a projected 12% annual increase in malaria‐related costs and an additional 48.5 million USD in economic losses [ 57 ]. Literature indicates low concentrations of ACT in East Africa, and it may contribute to the rapid spread of partial Artemisinin resistance. This leads to the death of millions of children until new alternative treatments to the ACT are available [ 38 ]. Several WHO‐candidate and validated molecular markers associated with Artemisinin resistance (ArtR) have been identified in Plasmodium falciparum populations across East and the Horn of Africa. Among these, the kelch13 622I (k13 622I) mutation has shown notable prevalence in Ethiopia and Eritrea, indicating emerging or established resistance patterns in these regions [ 58 ]. The R622I mutation has been detected in P. falciparum populations from Ethiopia and Eritrea, with recent findings indicating a notably high prevalence in northern Ethiopia [ 12 ]. This mutation was first reported in two small studies in the northwest part of Ethiopia (North Gondar) with increasing prevalence over 5 years, 2.4% in 2013 and 9.5% in 2017–18 [ 59 ]. A report from Rwanda indicated emerging Pfkelch13 mutations are compromising ACT efficacy. This may be contributing to decreasing Artemether‐lumefantrine therapeutic response [ 60 ]. A Ugandan study found that 22.5% of patients treated with ACTs experienced adverse drug reactions (ADRs), totaling 245 events. The most common ADRs were general body weakness (24%), headache (13%), and dizziness (11%). Women, urban residents, and patients with comorbidities were significantly more likely to develop ADRs [ 61 ]. Such occurrences may be attributed to a weak regulatory framework for post‐market surveillance and inspection, inadequate pharmacovigilance practices, and an ineffective antimalarial stewardship program. In the current context, ongoing armed conflicts further exacerbate the circulation of poor‐quality drugs as a result of illicit drug production, including ACT medicines [ 62 ]. 7.3. Efficacy and Safety Profiles 7.3.1. Number of Documents Reviewed Across the selected East Africa countries such as Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, 22 documents were reviewed. The studies conducted from 2003 to 2025 were included. These included randomised clinical trials, therapeutic efficacy monitoring studies, observation surveys, and molecular surveillance of resistance markers. The studies predominantly assessed uncomplicated falciparum malaria, though a few evaluated mixed infections ( P. falciparum and P. vivax ). The review found that, Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL) was the most widely studied regimen complemented by other ACTT's such as artesunate (AS) + artesunate‐amodiaquine (ASAQ), artesunate‐mefloquin (ASMQ), and dihydroartemisinin‐piperaquine (DHA/PPQ) (Table 2 ). 7.3.2. Efficacy Profiles and Population Involved In total, 45,769 patients and samples were included across the studies, comprising large observational datasets of 37,309 patients, smaller therapeutic trials ranging from 67 to 599 participants each, and 1199 molecular samples from Tanzania and Ethiopia, respectively (Table 4 ). Overall, efficacy measured by polymerase chain reaction (PCR)‐corrected adequate clinical and parasitological response (ACPR) remained consistently high (≥ 90%–100%) in most trials, meeting WHO thresholds for continued ACT use. Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL) demonstrated strong cure rates with rapid parasite and fever clearance, while dihydroartemisinin‐piperaquine (DHA/PPQ) showed superior prophylactic effects in some studies. Isolated treatment failures (5%–8%) were reported in Ethiopia, although their clinical relevance remains uncertain. While ACTs remain highly efficacious in East Africa, these findings indicate the pressing need for strengthened molecular surveillance, improved pharmacovigilance, and standardised therapeutic efficacy studies to sustain malaria control progress [ 81 ]. Regular monitoring of antimalarial drug efficacy is essential to guide treatment policies, while surveillance of molecular markers of resistance helps track its spread and signal when additional interventions are needed [ 82 ]. A comprehensive overview of both planned and ongoing efforts to collect efficacy and resistance data is therefore critical for prioritising resources and directing surveillance activities effectively [ 82 ]. 7.4. Regulatory Performance, Clinical Practice and Emerging Concerns Additionally, this review discussed the regulatory and policy framework, clinical practice and healthcare experiences, as well as emerging concerns, such as drug resistance resulting from poor‐quality Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) based on evidence retrieved from published literature. 7.4.1. Regulatory Performance Regulatory performance across East African countries exhibits substantial variability. In some contexts, strong frameworks and active programs support effective oversight. For example, Tanzania's Accredited Drug Dispensing Outlet (ADDO) program (2007–2008, 2014) demonstrates structured regulatory mechanisms, including training, supervision, record‐keeping, and targeted distribution of ACTs, which enhance both availability and adherence to treatment guidelines. Similarly, studies in Kenya (2021) and Uganda (2023) that adhered to WHO protocols indicate regulatory compliance in therapeutic efficacy assessments and molecular surveillance of malaria. However, enforcement remains inconsistent, and significant gaps persist. Cross‐sectional surveys across eight African countries (2009–2015) highlighted weak regulatory enforcement, with widespread circulation of non‐quality‐assured ACTs (non‐QAACTs) in the private sector. Reviews in Uganda (2023) and broader Sub‐Saharan Africa further emphasise reliance on international donors such as the Global Fund and limited local production, exposing systems to supply disruptions and inequitable access. Quality assurance issues also persist; a pharmacopoeia study in Uganda (2023) detected 18.9% substandard Artemether‐lumefantrine, particularly in high‐transmission regions, signalling weaknesses in regulatory oversight and post‐market surveillance. In Ethiopia, the regulatory performance for malaria treatment with Artemisinin‐based combination therapy (ACT), particularly Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL), has been consistently strong. As can be seen in Table 3 , therapeutic efficacy studies conducted in 2016 and 2024 demonstrate high cure rates (98.8% and 95.7%, respectively), confirming AL's status as the first‐line treatment and reflecting effective regulatory oversight and adherence to national treatment guidelines. Clinically, AL is well tolerated with only minor adverse effects reported, such as cough and oral ulceration, and treatment outcomes remain favourable. The review also found that emerging concerns primarily involve the potential for resistance development and occasional recrudescence, as well as limitations of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) in detecting all infections. These findings underline the importance of continuous efficacy monitoring, post‐market surveillance, and robust regulatory mechanisms to sustain treatment effectiveness and prevent the emergence of drug‐resistant malaria strains in Ethiopia. 7.4.2. Clinical Practice The review found that clinical practices in malaria treatment reveal a mixture of effective therapeutic outcomes and persistent challenges. As can be seen in Table 3 , across East African countries, first‐line Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs) such as Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL), artesunate‐amodiaquine (ASAQ), and dihydroartemisinin‐piperaquine (DHA‐PPQ) remain largely effective. Studies from Kenya (2013–2015) and Ethiopia (2016, 2024) demonstrate high cure rates and good tolerability, while Tanzanian data (2018) confirm ACTs' efficacy in the absence of validated k13 resistance markers. However, adherence challenges continue to undermine optimal outcomes. Additionally, cross‐sectional and qualitative studies indicate frequent overdiagnosis, non‐targeted ACT use, incomplete dosing, and reliance on clinical diagnosis without parasitological confirmation (Tanzania 2014; Uganda 2023). In addition, knowledge gaps and implementation barriers further complicate treatment, as indicated by interventions in Kenya (2023) and Uganda (2024) showing limited awareness of malaria‐in‐pregnancy (MiP) guidelines. Even in areas with relatively high baseline knowledge, poor ACT adherence persists due to frequent stockouts, system inefficiencies, and other logistical constraints, underscoring the need for ongoing training and strengthened health system support. Evidence from Uganda noted that healthcare personnel in Uganda report positive experiences with ACTs for malaria treatment, citing strong efficacy and the value of quality‐assured medicines. Nonetheless, challenges remain, particularly with diagnostic limitations and patient adherence [ 83 ]. In Kamuli District, community education initiatives have been implemented to enhance knowledge and optimise the use of ACTs, reflecting a broader effort to improve malaria treatment practices at the community level [ 84 ]. 7.4.3. Emerging Concern The review investigates that emerging challenges in malaria control in East Africa are closely linked to drug quality, resistance and systemic barriers. Findings indicate molecular surveillance in Uganda (2023) and Tanzania (2024) has detected emerging Artemisinin and piperaquinine resistance marked by PfK13 mutations, gene amplification and delayed parasite clearance; posing a critical threat to ACT efficacy. The circulation of poor quality medicines, including AL in Uganda and low quality QAACTs, further increases the risk of treatment failure and accelerates resistance development [ 85 ]. The review was also found that, the circulation of substandard or inappropriate medicines, including poor‐quality Artemether‐lumefantrine (AL) in Uganda and low‐quality Artemisinin combination therapy eight African countries including Est Africa countries, further increases the risk of treatment failure and accelerates resistance development. Operational and systemic challenges, such as stockouts, long distances to distributors, profit‐driven distribution of non‐ quality‐assured Artemisinin combination therapy (QAACTs), overuse in non‐malaria cases, false‐negative rapid diagnostic test (RDT) results, and high staff turnover, undermine treatment quality. Behavioural and communication gaps compound these risks, highlighting the need for community awareness campaigns and consistent healthcare worker training. Collectively, these factors contribute to non‐adherence, rising treatment failures, increased economic burden, and erosion of public trust in malaria control programs (Table 5 ). Policy Strategies to Mitigate Poor Quality, Clinical Concern, and Resistance Challenges This review synthesised evidence from 40 articles to propose policy strategies aimed at mitigating poor‐quality medicines, addressing clinical concerns, and tackling resistance challenges. Strengthening the regulatory framework is a critical step to mitigate the circulation of poor‐quality antimalarial medicines including Artemisinin‐based Combination Therapies (ACTs) in East Africa [ 93 ]. A similar suggestion discussed as a legal framework is the main actor in combating the quality and efficacy of ACTs [ 91 ]. National Medicines Regulatory Authorities (NMRAs) should adopt harmonised regional standards, expand post‐market surveillance, and implement risk‐based quality testing using WHO‐recommended protocols. Expanding initiatives such as Tanzania's Accredited Drug Dispensing Outlet (ADDO) program [ 94 ] and Kenya's pharmacovigilance reporting systems can serve as models to enhance medicine quality oversight and improve community‐level accountability [ 95 ]. Furthermore, adopting Quality by Design (QbD) principles in local manufacturing and ensuring procurement from prequalified suppliers can reduce the prevalence of substandard and falsified ACTs, thereby safeguarding therapeutic outcomes [ 51 ]. From a clinical perspective, strengthening treatment practices and surveillance systems is necessary to sustain antimalarials including ACT efficacy [ 96 ]. Regular therapeutic efficacy studies (TES), combined with molecular surveillance of resistance markers such as k13 polymorphisms and partner‐drug resistance genes, should be institutionalised across malaria‐endemic regions. Clinical guidelines should be reinforced through continuous healthcare worker training, supervision, and integration of digital health tools such as SMS adherence reminders and electronic reporting systems. These measures would not only ensure accurate diagnosis and adherence to treatment regimens but also enable early detection of treatment failures and resistance hotspots, thereby informing timely policy adjustments. Addressing the challenge of resistance also requires multifaceted strategies that integrate policy, health system, and community‐level interventions. Policies discouraging the sale and use of Artemisinin monotherapies should be strictly enforced [ 97 ], while promoting access to quality‐assured ACTs through public and private sectors. Community‐based education and awareness campaigns are essential to improve adherence, reduce self‐medication, and enhance trust in formal healthcare systems. At the same time, investment in local production capacity, regional procurement coordination, and sustained donor engagement can secure equitable access to high‐quality ACTs. These strategies, if implemented in synergy, can reduce the dual burden of poor‐quality medicines and resistance, thereby strengthening malaria control and accelerating progress toward elimination goals in East Africa. 8. Evidence‐Based Recommendations for Policymakers and Regulators This review suggests actionable recommendations for policymakers, regulatory agencies, and communities for sustainable malaria control in East Africa. Ministries of health should strengthen medicine quality assurance, postmarket surveillance enforcement, and harmonised regional regulatory frameworks. For instance, malaria burden is high in Ethiopia; to combat its health impact, the National Malaria Elimination Programme (NMEP) under the Ministry of Health oversees the design, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation of malaria interventions in Ethiopia [ 98 ]. On the medicine quality side, the country's regulatory agency, the Ethiopian Food, Medicine, and Health Care Administration and Control Authority (formerly the Ethiopian Food and Drug Authority), works with partners to promote the quality of medicines and strengthen regulatory quality assurance and postmarket surveillance of medicine products, including antimalarials. Since 2009, PQM has collaborated with the Ethiopian Food, Medicine, and Health Care Administration and Control Authority (EFMHACA), Ethiopian manufacturers, and other local partners to strengthen the country's medical product quality assurance systems, also working on increasing capacity to detect substandard, falsified, and unapproved medical products. Kenya's national malaria treatment guideline mandates that uncomplicated malaria be treated with ACT, for example, Artemether‐lumefantrine, as a first line. Since 2012, the policy has included parasitological confirmation via rapid diagnostic test or microscopy before initiating antimalarial therapy. However, implementation gaps remain; for instance, private drug outlets often do not have the national guidelines, and adherence is weak [ 99 ]. The findings gained from this study suggested that the Ministry of Health should enhance private sector engagement and train retail drug outlets and rapid diagnostic tools [ 99 ]. The regulatory body for pharmaceuticals in Kenya is the Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB) established under the Pharmacy and Poison Act, chapter 244. Evidence from Kenya indicates there was poor quality antimalarial drugs despite being registered by the Ministry of Health [ 100 ]. The evidence also noted that poor post‐market surveillance and recall systems indicate regulatory failure. The author suggests regulation will need to be strengthened to protect the market from banned substances and ineffective products, which pose a threat to the existence of falsified and substandard products [ 100 ]. Additionally, evidence from Kenya noted a lack of comparative efficacy data between combination antimalarial agent‐based alternatives. Additionally, poor negotiation with the pharmaceutical industry with a national interest in drug supply versus single sourcing of antimalarial drugs and complex drug ordering, tendering, and procurement procedures [ 101 ]. This may pose a challenge to changing the national malaria drug policy to Artemisinin‐based combinations [ 101 ]. Evidence from Tanzania indicate, 4.1% of Artemisinin derivatives in Artemisinin –containing antimalarial was out of specification of 85%–115% API range. When including the partner drug component for ACTs, about 12.1% outside acceptable API range [ 46 ]. Despite little quality failure, the Tanzanian regulatory system is robust, which is recognised by the WHO, as it is the first African country to reach an important milestone in the regulation of medicines [ 102 ]. The country is strengthening adverse drug reaction or pharmacovigilance systems for antimalarials to ensure the dispensers and private retail outlets are trained and reporting, as was piloted with accredited drug dispensing outlet [ 86 ]. Tanzania is working on harmonising and leveraging regional regulatory frameworks. As a member of the East African Community (EAC), Tanzania should contribute to aligning its medicine registration, inspection, and postmarket surveillance (PMS) with EAC‐Medicine Regulatory Harmonisation (MRH) frameworks. This may be reducing duplication, improving resource sharing, and enabling mutual recognition. Given the burden of malaria, the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare of Tanzania actively working on strengthening medicine quality assurance and regulatory harmonisation in context of first line treatment of uncomplicated Artemether–Lumefantrine (AL) and other Artemisinin‐based combination therapies (ACTs). Such robustness make Tanzania as main actor for motivating East African regulatory agencies for drawing relevance evidence and establishing implemented regional frameworks. Uganda's national policy of 2011 mandates parasite‐based diagnosis before treatment with antimalarials [ 103 ]. The first‐line treatment for uncomplicated malaria in Uganda is an ACT: Artemether/Lumefantrine (AL), with alternative first‐line being Artesunate/Amodiaquine (AS + AQ) and second‐line being Dihydroartemisinin‐Piperaquine (DHA‐PPQ) when needed [ 103 ]. Evidence shows that poor‐quality antimalarials, particularly substandard/falsified ACTs, have a major impact in Uganda: one modelling study estimated 71.3% of the economic burden from substandard/falsified antimalarials is attributable to low‐quality ACT [ 85 ]. Hence, establishing routine, independent sampling and testing of antimalarial products, particularly ACT's, in both health sectors is critical to detect substandard and falsified medicines. Even if the medicine affordability issue is the burden of patients, medicine quality failure occurs, and we should combat it. Given that many patients cannot afford the full ACT dose or stop early, which can drive treatment failures and resistance, subsidy mechanisms or co‐payment schemes should be maintained or scaled up. For example, Uganda uses a co‐payment mechanism with subsidies for quality‐assured Artemisinin‐based combination therapy (QAACT) medicines [ 83 ]. Hence, strengthening supply chain management and ensuring the availability of quality commodities should be prioritised. Additionally, linking data on drug quality with efficacy is important, as some treatment failures may be due to poor quality rather than parasitic resistance alone. Overall, looking forward, sustainable malaria control in East Africa will depend on harmonised regional policies, strengthened pharmacovigilance, and investment in both local production and regulatory capacity. Adoption of innovative strategies such as digital adherence tools, community‐based education, and molecular surveillance platforms will be critical in bridging clinical and regulatory gaps. Strict enforcement against Artemisinin monotherapies, coupled with donor‐supported but locally driven access strategies, can reduce the burden of substandard medicines and delay resistance. Ultimately, the future outlook requires a multifaceted, cross‐sectoral approach that ensures equitable access to quality‐assured ACTs, preserves therapeutic efficacy, and accelerates progress toward malaria elimination in the region. 9. Conclusion This systematic review highlights the dual challenges posed by substandard and falsified Artemisinin‐based Combination Therapies (ACTs) and the growing threat of Artemisinin resistance in East Africa. While the clinical efficacy of ACTs remains high, with most studies reporting PCR‐corrected cure rates above 90%, the circulation of poor‐quality medicines and the emergence of resistance‐associated molecular markers threaten these gains. Regulatory gaps, inadequate pharmacovigilance systems, and weak supply chain oversight continue to allow the infiltration of non‐quality‐assured ACTs, undermining both treatment outcomes and long‐term malaria control strategies. These findings underscore the need for a coordinated regional response that integrates regulatory strengthening, clinical monitoring, and resistance surveillance to safeguard ACT effectiveness. 10. Strength and Limitation This systematic review draws on a wide range of data sources of published articles, including peer‐reviewed articles, thereby providing a comprehensive synthesis of the quality, clinical efficacy, and regulatory performance of Artemisinin‐based Combination Therapies (ACTs) in East Africa. The inclusion of both Pharmacopeial quality studies and therapeutic efficacy trials allows for an integrated understanding of how medicine quality, clinical outcomes, and resistance dynamics intersect. By adhering to PRISMA guidelines and employing established methodological tools such as MEDQUARG and STROBE, the review ensures transparency, methodological rigour, and reliability of findings. Moreover, the focus on multiple East African countries enables cross‐country comparisons that highlight contextual variations and provide regionally relevant policy recommendations. Despite these strengths, several limitations should be acknowledged. The qualitative nature of the review precluded meta‐analysis and limited the ability to generate pooled prevalence estimates of poor‐quality ACTs or resistance markers. Variability in study designs, sampling strategies, and outcome definitions across the included studies introduced heterogeneity, which complicates direct comparisons between countries and times. In addition, some studies lacked PCR correction, molecular marker analysis, or robust genotyping, limiting the accuracy of distinguishing true treatment failures from reinfections. Furthermore, gaps in pharmacovigilance reporting and limited long‐term molecular surveillance data in the region restrict the ability to fully assess trends in emerging resistance. documents.title: Urban malaria and population mobility in sub-Saharan Africa: systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malaria control in African cities faces challenges mainly due to rapid and unplanned urbanization and the spread of the new urban malaria vector, Anopheles stephensi. By 2050, nearly 70% of the world`s population will live in urban areas, a significant increase from the current rate. This systematic review and meta-analysis map the epidemiology of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). The review included individual participants data from studies conducted in urban settings among all populations to characterize and establish pooled estimates of the prevalence and risk factors, which would help guiding strategies for malaria control and elimination in urban settings.
METHODS: An exhaustive literature search was done in PubMed, Medline EBSCO, Google Scholar, Science Direct, and Cochrane Library databases. The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) guidelines were followed for evidence selection, data extraction, quality assessment and presentation of findings. Peer-reviewed and gray literature published in English since 2000 focusing on urban malaria Epidemiology in SSA was included in the review. Microsoft Excel 2016 spreadsheet and Stata statistical package were used to extract and analyze data, respectively. Potential sources of heterogeneity and publication bias were assessed. A random effects model was employed for the meta- analysis.
RESULTS: Of the 2,468 records identified from various databases, 39 articles were selected for systematic review and meta-analysis. The overall pooled prevalence of urban malaria in SSA was 23.01% (95% CI: 19.42, 26.59; I2 = 99.8%, p 2 = 99.8%), indicating considerable variability in population and methods employed. Among two studies included for analysis, a random effect model showed that odds of malaria infection were higher among study participants who had history of travel (POR = 4.17 (95% CI: 2.33, 7.46, I2 = 75.5%, p = 0.002). Similarly, five studies were included in the review and showed that owning livestock in the house was associated with malaria infection in urban settings (POR = 4.1, 95% CI: 1.62, 10.39; I2 = 75.3%, p = 0.044).
CONCLUSION: This systematic review and meta-analysis showed a high prevalence of urban malaria infection in SSA with high country-wise heterogeneity. While country-level differences contributed to this variability, other important sources of heterogeneity included variations in population included, method employed and population characteristics. The pooled estimate showed that having a travel history and owning livestock in the house were identified as factors associated with urban malaria infection. Therefore, effective urban malaria control requires an integrated and targeted approach that addresses socio-economic, environmental and behavioural drivers.

Background Malaria is a life-threatening disease primarily found in tropical countries and continues to have a great impact on people’s health and livelihoods globally, even though it is preventable and treated. The World Health Organization (WHO) World Malaria Report 2024 indicated that an estimated 263 million malaria cases were reported globally—an increase of 11 million cases from the 2023 report. The WHO African Region remained the most affected, accounting for 94% of all cases [ 1 , 2 ]. By 2050, nearly 70% of the global population will live in cities. The WHO and UN-Habitat (United Nations Human Settlements Programme) warn that while urbanization offers benefits, rapid and unplanned growth can harm health, society, and the environment [ 3 ]. The global patterns of disease and mortality, including malaria, will change due to a shift in human population from rural to urban areas [ 4 ]. Urbanization has altered health patterns in certain places, making infectious disease risks in urban environments different from those in rural ones [ 5 ]. Malaria control in urban environments of Africa is also challenged by the recent invasion and expansion of Anopheles stephensi as well as rapid and poorly designed urbanization. Anopheles stephensi , an urban malaria vector, was recently introduced to Africa from its native Asia [ 6 ]. This vector reproduces in artificial water storage containers, withstands extreme temperatures, and resists multiple insecticides; its uncontrolled spread, combined with rapid urbanization, could drive malaria outbreaks in African cities [ 7 – 13 ]. Several models have predicted the widespread of the disease in urban areas, where it may trigger severe malaria outbreaks among the expanding resident populations [ 10 , 11 , 13 , 14 ]. There is little agreement over what constitutes an urban area or how to define the urbanization process. While size and density are used in certain nations, administrative definitions are used in others. Despite problems with the definition of what constitutes urban, most urban settings in SSA are now viewed as presenting an increased risk of various infectious diseases including malaria [ 4 , 5 , 15 ]. Urbanization is generally expected to reduce malaria transmission; however, the disease still persists in African cities, in some cases at higher levels than in nearby rural areas [ 9 ]. Urban malaria is the transmission of malaria within urban areas mainly influenced by unplanned urbanization and the emergence of urban mosquito vectors. Evidence from sub-Saharan Africa demonstrated that urban malaria transmission differs significantly from district to district within a populous area, and the focal character of transmission necessitates a careful assessment of the risk in different cities [ 16 ]. Although some studies showed that urbanization reduced malaria morbidity and mortality [ 4 , 17 – 19 ], more recent research indicates urbanization increases the risk of malaria transmission, particularly following the spread of urban malaria vector species [ 5 ]. A study on the impact of urbanization and population density in Africa examined how these factors influence the risk of contracting malaria. The findings revealed a persistent threat of malaria infection in densely populated urban areas across the African continent [ 20 ]. Similarly, research from Benin and Ghana highlighted the continued transmission of urban malaria [ 21 , 22 ]. On the other hands, population mobility or history of travel is the major risk factor for urban malaria transmission. Various studies have indicated that a history of travel significantly increases the odds of malaria morbidity and mortality [ 5 , 23 – 26 ]. For malaria control strategies to be effective, urban areas where infections are occurring must be targeted, with success relying on accurate epidemiological data [ 5 ]. Over the past two decades (2000 to 2024), numerous studies have examined the prevalence and determinants of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa using various approaches. These studies, conducted under different ecological conditions, among diverse populations, and with varying sample sizes, sampling methods, and diagnostic techniques, have led to considerable heterogeneity in malaria positivity rate and risk factors. A systematic review and meta-analysis provide a valuable and efficient approach to obtaining a weighted estimate. Therefore, this study aims to assess the pooled prevalence and risk factors of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa since 2000. Especially, it seeks to answer the following specific research questions: 1) what is the current prevalence and incidence of urban malaria in SSA? 2) what are the key risk factors associated with urban malaria transmission? A clear understanding of these factors is crucial for making informed decisions to support both global and regional malaria elimination strategy. Methods This systematic review was conducted using framework recommended by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) for systematic review of prevalence and etiologic studies [ 27 ]. Inclusion criteria The eligibility criteria were based on the JBI framework. A comprehensive search strategy was designed to identify relevant literature, following established frameworks. It was developed based on the “CoCoPo” mnemonic (Concept–Context-population) for systematic reviews of prevalence studies and the “PEO” mnemonic (Population-Exposure of interest-Outcome) for etiologic studies, as recommended by the Joanna Briggs Institute. The mnemonics aligns with this specific research questions and provides significant information for readers. This framework was ‘Population (urban residents), Concept (urban malaria), outcome (malaria infection) and Context (sub-Saharan Africa)’. The Population encompassed all individuals, regardless of age and sex, living in urban settings. The Concept focused on urban malaria, incorporating all related investigations or studies, irrespective of the malaria parasite species. Malaria prevalence or incidence of any species was considered as an outcome in this review. The Context considered sub-Saharan Africa and the countries within this region. Searching sources and search strategy To conduct this review, a three-step search strategy was employed to identify both published and unpublished studies. First, relevant literature was gathered from various accessible databases including PubMed, Google Scholar, Cochrane Library, Medline EBSCO, and other sources of gray literature. Second, a comprehensive search strategy was developed using Medical Subject Heading (MeSH), indexed terms, and specific keywords derived from the research question. Third, supplementary searches were conducted, including gray literature searches, citation tracking, and hand-searching. All published and unpublished studies assessing urban malaria were retrieved from multiple databases including websites of various national and international organizations. Only studies published in English since 2000 were included. This search strategy involved combining specific terms across different databases (Table 1 ). The search strategy and results for PubMed data base is attached as supplementary file (S1). Two independent reviewers (HM & TD) then screened the remaining articles in two stages: first by title and abstract, and then by full-text review. Abstracts were excluded from the initial screening if they did not report the prevalence of urban malaria or its determinants. Studies that met the inclusion criteria were assessed for methodological quality and only those articles with high quality standards were included in the meta-analysis. Moreover, the papers were also searched outside the search strategy using cross-referencing and contacting experts in the area. Furthermore, additional relevant articles were identified outside the primary search strategy through cross-referencing and consultation with experts in the field. Any disagreements during the review were solved through discussion or with additional reviewer (DY). This systematic review considered observational studies mainly prospective and retrospective cohort, case–control and cross-sectional studies. It did not consider case series, individual case reports and correlational studies. Moreover, qualitative studies, literature review, systematic reviews, text and opinion papers were not considered. Quality assessment and critical appraisal For quality assessment, Joanna Briggs Institute's study-specific critical appraisal tool was used [ 28 ]. The tool consists of 9 criteria presented as questions, which can be answered with “yes”, “No”, “Not reported”, or “Not appropriate”. Based on the proportion of ‘yes’ response to the appraisal questions, the studies were categorized into three groups: low, moderate, and high risk of bias. The maximum score a paper could attain was 9 or 100%. The final score was divided by 9 to get the quality index of each paper. A study with 80% or more “yes” responses to the relevant questions, indicating good methodological quality, was classified as having a “low” risk of bias. Studies with 60% to 79% “yes” responses, suggesting some methodological limitations, were classified as having a “moderate” risk of bias. Lastly, studies with fewer than 60% “yes” responses, raising significant concerns about their quality, were deemed as having a “high” risk of bias. Papers with a rating above 50% were included in the final analysis. The critical appraisal results for the screened studies in this research are listed in Table 2 . The meta-analysis was performed using Stata statistical software version 16 (Stata Corp., College Station, TX, USA). During the analysis, potential sources of heterogeneity were explored through sub-group analysis as well as meta regression, and publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot. The Cochrane Q test and Inconsistency index (I 2 statistics) were used to evaluate the heterogeneity among the studies. Heterogeneity was observed for the outcome; therefore, a random-effects model was used to determine the pooled prevalence of urban malaria infection. A Cochrane Q value with p < 0.05 indicated significant heterogeneity. Heterogeneity levels were categorized as low, moderate, and high based on I 2 values of less than 25%, 25–75%, and greater than 75%, respectively. Forest plots were used to display point estimates and confidence intervals. Publication bias was evaluated visually through funnel plots (subjectively) and statistically using Egger’s and Begg’s tests (objectively). A p-value > 0.05 indicates no evidence of publication bias. Trim-and-fill analysis was conducted to estimate the number of studies potentially missing due to publication bias, impute those studies, and derive the overall effect size using both observed and imputed data. Results Selection and characteristics of included studies A total of 2468 of published and unpublished articles related to the title were accessed in this initial literature search. After removing 343 duplicate articles, 2125 articles were screened for title and abstract relevance. For full text review, 106 articles were eligible. Finally, after a comprehensive reading of relevant sections of those articles, 39 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis as shown on PRISMA below (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow chart diagram for prevalence of Urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa This systematic review of the prevalence studies included a total of 233,425 study participants with 34,946 confirmed cases. The majority of the studies were cross-sectional, used for estimating pooled prevalence, while both cross-sectional and case–control studies were utilized to examine determinants. Studies from 16 countries from sub-Saharan Africa were included in the study. Ethiopia contributed the largest proportion of prevalence studies (21.2%), with a sample size of 181,533 and 22,593 confirmed cases, followed by Cameroon (15.15%) with a sample size of 1,234 and 434 confirmed cases. Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax were the predominant malaria species reported in the studies included in this review (Table 3 ). Pooled prevalence of urban malaria Substantial heterogeneity was found among included articles (I 2 = 99.8%, p < 0.0001), and a random-effects model was used to estimate the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in SSA. The overall pooled prevalence was 23.01% (95% CI: 19.42, 26.59) (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 A forest plot showing the pooled prevalence estimate of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, 2025 Sub-group analysis and meta regression analysis To assess heterogeneity among the included studies, sub-group analysis and meta regression was conducted by diagnostic methods (RDT (Rapid Diagnostic Test), Microscopy and PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)) employed, study settings, year of publication and study population. The meta-regression analysis revealed that the type of diagnostic method significantly influences the estimated malaria prevalence, with studies using PCR reporting higher prevalence rates (effect size = 0.275, p = 0.009; 95% CI: 0.1, 0.5). In contrast, other factors—such as study year, use of RDT, and study population type—were not significantly associated with malaria prevalence (p > 0.05), indicating they had no substantial impact on the effect size in this analysis (Fig. 3 ). Fig. 3 Meta regression analysis Accordingly, the highest pooled prevalence was reported among those tested with PCR (53.37%, 95% CI: 35.13, 71.62%, I 2 = 96.5%, p < 0.0001) followed by Microscopy (21.88%, 95% CI: 17.89, 25.87%, I 2 = 99.8%, p < 0.00010) and RDT (9.39.88%, 95% CI: − 2.01, 20.79, I 2 = 99%, p < 0.0001). Heterogeneity is high among those sub-groups (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 4 Sub-group analysis by diagnostic methods for the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in SSA Similarly, subgroup analysis by publication year (since the detection of An. stephensi in Africa) (before 2012 and 2012 & onwards) was conducted. Even though the heterogeneity was high and similar in both categories, the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in 2012 and onwards was higher (24.01%; 95% CI: 20.14, 27.89.13, I 2 = 99.8%, p < 0.0001) than before 2012 (20.19%, 95%CI: 8.47, 31.92, I 2 = 99.8%, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5 Sub-group analysis by year of publication for the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, 2025 In this meta-analysis, subgroup analysis was also conducted using study settings. The pooled prevalence of studies conducted in school (among school children) 33.4% (95% CI: 1.93, 64.94) was higher than health facility 27.10% (95% CI: 21.86, 32.34) and community based 13.65% (95%CI: 9.61, 17.69) pooled prevalences (Fig. 6 ). Fig. 6 Sub-group analysis by study setting for the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, 2025 The sub-group analysis by study population indicated that the pooled prevalence among children was 33.33% (95% CI: 21.01, 45.66), among pregnant mothers 28.79% (95% CI: 24.35, 33.23), among households 25.06% (95% CI: 19.69, 30.42) and among febrile patients 13.65% (95% CI: 9.61, 17.69) (Fig. 7 ). Fig. 7 Sub-group analysis by study population for the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, 2025 A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the effect of each study on the malaria prevalence pooled estimate. It is revealed that the size remained consistent around and none of the studies seems to be an extreme outlier that shifts the overall pooled estimate significantly (Fig. 8 ). Fig. 8 Sensitivity analysis graph to examine the effect of each study on the pooled prevalence of urban malaria in sub-Saharan Africa, 2025 Assessment of publication bias To generate a funnel plot, the effect of the study was plotted against the standard error (Fig. 8 A). The visual evaluation of the funnel plot in this picture showed an asymmetrical picture. However, due to its subjectivity in evaluating the presence of publication bias, Egger’s test and Begg’s test were performed and the results showed absence of statistical evidence of publication bias (Egger’s test, coefficient = 7.71, 95% CI: − 1.49 to 16.91, p = 0.098 and Begg’s test statistic of z = 2.01 and p = 0.076) (Fig. 9 ). Trim-and-fill analysis suggested that there is no study imputed to account for potential publication bias. There is no indication that studies with different results are missing from the analysis (Fig. 9 B). Fig. 9 Funnel plot and trim and fill analysis for assessment of publication bias Factors associated with urban malaria infection in sub-Saharan Africa In this review, several variables from primary studies were reviewed to see their association with malaria infection. Thus, four variables that predicted urban malaria infection (travel history, stagnant water, ITN utilization and owning Livestock) were reviewed. However, only two of them (travel history and owning livestock) found statistically significant for malaria infection (Table 4 ).
