Background The burden of malaria is lower than ten years ago. However, in the last few years, there has been an increase in the number of malaria cases around the world. It is moving towards targets established by the World Health Organization (WHO), but that progress has slowed down [ 1 ]. In Africa today, malaria is understood to be both a disease of poverty and a cause of poverty. The association between poverty and malaria has been demonstrated elsewhere [ 1 – 3 ]. Malaria has significant measurable direct and indirect costs, and has been shown to be a major constraint to economic development. The direct costs of malaria include a combination of personal and public expenditures on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the disease. The indirect costs of malaria include lost productivity or income associated with illness or death [ 1 ]. Measuring the economic cost of malaria is critical for policymakers to set priorities, allocate resources, select control and prevention strategies, and evaluate the efficiency of interventions taken to control and eliminate malaria. A number of primary studies have been conducted in different countries of Africa to quantify the costs of malaria [ 4 – 8 ]. However, their findings are variable since they assessed the value of costs with different cost perspectives, cost components (categories), and varied target population groups. As per the extensive searching of scientific databases, two reviews were conducted in Africa on the cost of malaria. The first was a study by Chima et al . [ 9 ], which was a critical review of studies on the economic impact of malaria. It showed the limitations of cost of illness (COI) studies on malaria conducted before. Accordingly, studies were generally focussed on febrile illness, overestimating the burden of uncomplicated malaria but underestimating the costs of severe illness; many of them used limited data to calculate indirect costs, which fail to account for seasonal variations. The second was a systematic review conducted in 2019 [ 10 ] to assess the economic and resource use associated with management of malaria in children aged less than five years in sub-Saharan Africa. The review assessed and presented the health system cost of malaria treatment for the inpatient and outpatient cases as well as household treatment costs. Each of the previous reviews were with noticeable limitations; the former was not based on systematic searching and review protocol and the latter was restricted on presenting only the treatment cost of malaria. More importantly the review by Andrade et al . [ 12 ] observed the cost of malaria from different perspectives (household, health system perspectives, societal) by considering countries around the world. The review tried to show the economic burden of malaria prevention and treatments on different countries though the studies included to the review were restricted to the year 2020 and hence it could limit to include more studies from African countries, where malaria is known to be epidemic. Subsequently, this makes it hard to translate the findings to the present. This study aimed to systematically review articles on the cost of malaria conducted specifically in Africa. The review was conducted by including studies that was published since 2000 to 2024 and assessed the cost of malaria with different perspectives such as health system, household, and societal perspectives. It also analysed studies that were conducted to assess the cost of malaria with different cost components (categories) like direct cost of malaria (could be for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment) and indirect costs associated with productivity losses due the malaria illness. Finally, the results of the included studies were presented and well described. Methods A systematic review of studies in Africa on the cost of malaria was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA 2020) guideline [ 12 ]. Eligibility criteria We included studies published since 2000 to 2024 and conducted in African countries, assessed costs of malaria for (prevention, diagnosis, and treatment) from the health service provider, the household, and societal perspectives. On the other hand, studies that missed to present the cost of malaria clearly and involve only economic evaluation methods, conducted in private sectors, reviews (not primary studies), and epidemiological studies which assessed the burden and distribution of malaria were excluded. Information source, searching methods, and study selection Studies were retrieved after systematic searching with Google scholar, Cochrane Library, and PubMed databases. Using the PECO framework (Population, Exposure, Comparator, and Out comes), both simple and advanced searching techniques in each of the databases using key words as well as Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms was employed. Search terms such as Malaria, plasmodium, “malaria illness”, “epidemic malaria”, “febrile illness, Cost, “economic burden”, and “cost of illness” were used. The PECO framework, the search terms used in all the data bases, and terms with Boolean operators applied in the PubMed advanced search are listed in Additional file 1 . The electronic search was complemented by hand-searching of the related articles as well as the reference lists of the selected studies. After the intensive searching and retrieval of the studies, the reference lists of the search results were imported to Endnote version X9 reference manager. Duplicates were first removed electronically and then manually. The title and abstract of the studies were independently screened by all authors, and irrelevant studies were removed. Subsequently, the full text of included studies was reviewed against the inclusion criteria for further screening and disagreement on whether to include articles if they fulfil some inclusion criteria but not the whole was finally resolved by consensus. Data extraction, data analysis, and study quality assessment A customized Microsoft Excel template was used to abstract detailed information about each study’s publication year, study area, study perspective (household, health system, and societal), cost categories (direct medical cost for malaria prevention/diagnosis/treatment, direct non-medical, and indirect cost), unit of measurement (cost per case, per household, per unit/episode), and the value of the cost with United States Dollar (USD) or the currency of the country where the study was conducted. Anteneh Lamesgen and Mamo Engidaw performed the data extraction and to facilitate comparison, all cost values were converted into Purchase Power Parity 2024 American dollars (PPP-USD) using the Campbell and Cochrane Economics Methods Group (CCEMG)—Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Coordinating Centre (EPPI Centre) cost converter [ 13 ]. Tables and charts were used to describe the characteristics of studies in terms of their publication years, study perspectives (household, health system, societal), their cost categories (direct medical cost for malaria prevention/diagnosis/treatment and indirect cost), and unit of cost measurements. The values of costs in each study perspective and cost categories were analysed using minimum and maximum values (range of cost values). Results Study selection process A total of 1433 articles were initially identified through the primary search using google scholar, Cochrane Library, and PubMed databases. Eighty-seven articles were removed due to duplicates, 1292 articles were found irrelevant based on their titles and abstracts. Fifty-four studies were reviewed against the eligibility criteria. Subsequently, 10 articles were excluded (three of them missed to present the cost of malaria clearly and involve economic evaluation methods [ 14 – 16 ], two studies conducted in private sectors [ 17 , 18 ], two articles were reviews (not primary studies) [ 19 , 20 ], and three were epidemiologic studies assessing the burden and distribution of malaria [ 21 – 23 ]. The reference lists of the selected articles were manually searched, but no additional studies were found. The PRISMA flow diagram was used [ 24 ] for screening and selecting studies. Finally, 44 published articles were included in this review (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Flow chart for the systematic search and study selection proccess Characteristics of the studies Studies included in this review covered nineteen African countries. Five studies involved a cross-country comparison [ 4 , 25 – 28 ]. This review includes studies which analysed the cost of malaria from different perspectives. While 18 (41%) of the studies observed the cost of malaria from the household perspective, 24 (54.5%) of them assessed the cost from the health system perspective, and only two articles assessed the cost of malaria from both the house hold and the health system perspective [ 4 , 7 ] (Table 1 ). between the years 2001 and 2023 and more than half of them (57%) were published after 2015. Four studies were published in 2023 [ 26 , 27 , 37 , 52 ] (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Distribution of studies included in the review along with their publication year Generally, all of the selected studies fulfilled most the items that should be included in cost of illness studies (Additional file 2 ). However, there were studies missed to fulfil few items; some of the studies missed to describe the methods of costing approaches, and some of them did not clearly state the cost categories. Household costs of malaria Almost all studies which assessed the cost of malaria from the household perspective assessed the treatment costs. From the household perspective, the treatment cost of malaria was analysed with each of the cost categories and level of severity for malaria. The total treatment cost for simple (uncomplicated) malaria per case ranged from USD 4.03 [ 40 ] to USD 31.23 [ 26 ] and for the severe malaria, it ranged from USD 10.48 [ 67 ] to USD 70.86 [ 40 ]. Besides this, the total treatment cost per household ranged from USD 5.1 [ 46 ] to USD 19 [ 30 ]. The direct cost of malaria treatment per case ranged from USD 1.66 [ 34 ] to USD 20.75 [ 28 ] and the indirect cost per case ranged from USD 2.28 [ 38 ] to USD 37.54 [ 4 ] (Table 1 ). Health system and societal cost of malaria Studies which assessed the cost of malaria from the health system perspective analysed the cost for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of malaria. The cost incurred for malaria prevention was mainly for insecticide-treated bed nets distribution, microbial management using larvicide, and house management using indoor residual spraying; whereas the cost for malaria diagnosis was mainly for RDT. The maximum preventive cost for insecticide-treated bed nets distribution per unit ITN, larvicide per individual, and indoor residual spraying per a single use was about USD 10.81 [ 56 ], USD 28.43 [ 33 ], and USD 18.55 [ 43 ], respectively. The study by Tsehay et al . [ 29 ] indicated that the cost for the diagnosis of malaria using rapid diagnostic test was about 5.6 USD per a single RDT test (Table 1 ). The maximum health system cost for the treatment of malaria per a single case was estimated to be USD 262.17 [ 55 ]. In this review, two studies assessed the treatment cost of malaria from the societal perspective. According to the studies, the total treatment cost of malaria was USD 66.62 in Watts et al. [ 7 ] and USD 78.08 in Sicuri et al . [ 4 ]. Discussion This review presented the result of synthesized evidence from studies on the costs of malaria published since 2000 in the African continent. Forty-four studies covering nineteen African countries were reviewed systematically following the PRISMA guideline. The different cost categories of malaria were assessed with household, health system, and societal perspectives by the included studies. The total treatment cost for simple (uncomplicated) malaria per case ranged from USD 4.03 [ 40 ] to USD 31.23 [ 26 ] and for the sever malaria, it ranged from USD 10.48 [ 67 ] to USD 70.86 [ 40 ]. This difference might be due to the use of different costing methods across the different studies, or the use of different malaria treatment guidelines across countries. As we can observe here, the treatment cost of sever malaria is almost two times for uncomplicated malaria. This can show us the potential benefits of early management and prevention efforts for minimizing the extra costs by preventable diseases in general. Studies from the review also revealed that the minimum direct cost of malaria treatment per case was 1.3 USD whereas the minimum indirect cost of malaria treatment per case was about 2.28 USD. This finding is consistent with studies in Ethiopia [ 38 ] and Uganda [ 68 ] where the indirect cost of malaria treatment was higher than its direct cost. This might be due to the loss of productivity (absent from work) and experiencing inactive working days due to the physical and mental discomforts developed by the malaria illness that increases the indirect costs. The higher figure on the indirect costs of malaria is the productivity loss due to the illness and this can show as the negative effect of such infectious diseases on the economic growth of individuals, a country, and the continent at large. This is supported by previous evidences that revealed the association of malaria with poverty [ 69 ]. The cost for malaria prevention via ITN distribution and costs incurred for diagnosing malaria using the RDT test from the health system perspective were presented by the included studies. While the cost per unit ITN distribution varied across studies, the cost per unit RDT test was almost similar in each study. This might be due to the use of different number of resources for the ITN distribution among different setups but the inputs for RDT test could not be varied. Compared to the previous reviews on the cost of malaria [ 9 – 11 ] that were conducted to review studies mainly on the treatment costs of malaria and limited to the publication year of the studies to 2020, this review was conducted by including studies that were published since 2000 to 2024 and assessed the cost of malaria with different perspectives such as health system, household, and societal perspectives. The cost of malaria prevention and diagnosis with the type of intervention for each cost components from the studies included to this systematic review were also observed. The review examined articles on the cost of malaria conducted specifically in Africa. This review has a limitation on synthesizing the cost of malaria from the included studies using meta-analysis. This is due to the variation in the cost data across studies in terms of the study perspective (household, health system, and societal), the cost category considered in each study (direct and indirect costs), and the cost components (cost for malaria prevention/diagnosis/treatment). Nevertheless, the review examined the different studies on the cost of malaria and presented using descriptive statistical methods for the different cost components as well as based on varied intervention types. This can be an important input for health care planners and policy makers in all countries to design appropriate strategies on the prevention and control of malaria. Conclusions Overall, this review provides a good information on the cost of malaria in African. It showed the remarkable costs incurred for managing malaria illness in different perspectives (patient, health system, and societal) and this can indicate the invaluable role of prevention measures for malaria to the growth and development of the continent. Due attention is required while using the result and interpreting it. the cost variability across studies might be accounted for either the use of different costing methods, spatial variation, or the population considered while estimating the cost for malaria. Beside this, in some of the studies the number and value inputs used in the cost analysis, the cost categories, and the methods of costing approaches were not clearly stated. To synthesis the cost data using meta-analysis, studies on the COI require to follow uniform costing methods and considering the discount rates while calculating health service costs. It can also facilitate meaningful comparison of cost estimates and to apply the results for evidence-based practices. documents.title: Prevalence of sickle cell disease and sickle cell traits among children and adolescents in Nigeria: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is one of the most common genetic disorders in the world, with Nigeria believed to have the highest burden. Despite the high burden in the country, the true prevalence of SCD and its main driver-the sickle cell trait (SCT)-is unknown, which is important for planning and resource allocation. Hence, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the prevalence of SCD, SCT, and associated factors in Nigerian children and adolescents.
METHODS: Using the PRISMA guidelines [ID: CRD42024556354], we systematically search the following major databases: AJOL, Google Scholar, PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science collections from January 1950 to October 2024 on Nigerian children and adolescents with SCD and/or SCT. The quality of the studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale adapted for cross-sectional studies. We performed a cumulative meta-analysis to estimate the pooled prevalence and associated factors for SCD and SCT.
RESULTS: Thirty studies, comprising 211,938 participants, were included in the final analysis after stepwise screening. The pooled prevalences of SCD and SCT were 4.0% (95% CI 3.0 to 6.0, I2 = 99.6%) and 21.0% (95% CI 20.0 to 23.0, I2 = 90.5%), respectively. The northwestern geopolitical zone had the highest pooled prevalence of SCD (7.0%; 95% CI 3.0 to 11.0; I2 = 98.9%) and SCT (23.0%; 95% CI 19.0 to 28.0%, I2 = 54.2%). The southeastern region had the lowest pooled prevalence of SCD (2.0%, 95% CI 0.3 to 3.0%, I2 = 96.5), whereas the southwestern region had the lowest pooled prevalence of SCT (19.0%, 95% CI 14.0 to 25.0%, I2 = 92.2). There was no relationship between sex, socioeconomic status, and SCD.
CONCLUSION: The pooled prevalence of SCD and SCT among children and adolescents was high, with the highest burden occurring in the northwestern geopolitical zone in Nigeria. In addition, there was no relationship between sex, socioeconomic class, and prevalence of SCD.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO ID: CRD42024556354.

Keywords: Sickle cell disease, Sickle cell trait, Prevalence, Children, Adolescents, Nigeria status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Received 2025 May 6; Accepted 2025 Dec 7; Collection date 2026. Introduction Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common genetic blood disorder with significant impacts on the lives of millions of affected individuals and their families [ 1 , 2 ]. With an estimated eight million affected individuals, SCD affects all regions of the world with varying burdens and impacts [ 1 ]. The recent estimate of the global burden of SCD represents a 41.0% increase in the prevalence of SCD between 2010 and 2021, partly attributable to the increase in population dynamics [ 1 , 2 ]. The greater burden of SCD, including its main driver—sickle cell traits (SCT)—disproportionately affects sub-Saharan Africa, where its impact is profound and multifaceted, encompassing a complex interplay of medical, social, economic, and cultural factors [ 3 ]. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for 5.7 million global cases of SCD and 50 to 90% of related deaths among children with SCD without access to comprehensive healthcare [ 1 , 4 ]. In addition, a greater variation exists in the documented prevalence of SCD within the sub-regions. For instance, the prevalence of SCD in East Africa ranges from 0.8% among infants in Kenya [ 5 ] to 3.0% in Western Uganda [ 6 ]. In the West African sub-region, the estimated prevalence of SCT was 20–30%, far higher than the pooled prevalence of 5.9% reported in a recent systematic review in India [ 7 ]. Of the estimated 400,000 babies born in Africa with SCD, Nigeria contributed the highest burden with an estimated 150,000 babies, making SCD a disease of significant priority in Nigeria [ 8 , 9 ]. In Nigeria, researchers have also documented varying prevalence rates across different geopolitical zones, ranging from 0.3 to 5.0% [ 10 – 12 ]. For instance, a recent community-based investigation spanning 29 primary healthcare centers in the northcentral and northwest regions indicated a SCD prevalence of 3.2% and 2.7%, respectively [ 13 ]. In contrast, in southeastern Nigeria, the hospital prevalence of SCD is estimated to be 5.0% [ 12 ]. Although studies on the prevalence of SCD among children and adolescents in Nigeria have been conducted across various subpopulations and settings, such as hospitals and communities with significant variations, the actual national prevalence remains unknown, hampering adequate planning and resource allocation [ 12 , 14 ]. In addition, an important driver of the high burden of SCD is the presumed high rate of the sickle cell trait (SCT), with the exact burden also unknown, despite various efforts to reduce the burden of both SCD and SCT in Nigeria. Hence, there is a need to identify the pooled prevalence nationwide and establish regional burdens and associated factors. We therefore raised the following research questions: What is the pooled prevalence of sickle cell disease (SCD) and sickle cell trait (SCT) among Nigerian children and adolescents? Is there a regional variation in the prevalence of SCD and SCT among children and adolescents across the six geopolitical zones in Nigeria? What is the relationship between SCD and sociodemographic factors (sex and socioeconomic status) in Nigeria? Is there a difference between the community- and hospital-based prevalence of SCD in Nigeria? Therefore, this study aimed to document the pooled national and regional prevalence rates and the sociodemographic factors related to SCD and SCT among Nigerian children and adolescents through a systematic review and meta-analysis. Materials and methods This study was prepared and written based on the PRISM (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) checklist 2020 (Supplementary material 1) [ 15 ]. Protocol and registration The protocol for this systematic review and meta-analysis was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (Prospero ID: CRD42024556354) before the commencement of this review and was published in the Nigerian Journal of Pediatrics [ 16 ]. Eligibility criteria The ‘PICOS’ framework was used to define the eligibility criteria for the studies included as follows. Population (P): we included published studies on Nigerian newborns, children, and adolescents aged day 0 of life to 19 years with sickle cell disease and/or traits residing in the country. Intervention (I)-Not applicable. Comparator (C): We compared the groups and subgroups according to age, sex, socioeconomic status, years of study, study designs, study settings [hospital-based vs. community-based], and methods of diagnosis. O (Outcomes): our primary outcome was the pooled prevalence of SCD and SCT among children and adolescents in Nigeria. The secondary outcomes included the regional variation in the prevalence of SCD and SCT in Nigeria based on the country’s six geopolitical regions [northwest, northeast, northcentral, south-south, southeast, and southwest], sex variation in the prevalence of SCD among children in Nigeria, the relationship between socioeconomic class and SCD in Nigeria, and subgroup analysis of the prevalence of SCD [based on the study design, study settings, age groups, methods of diagnosis, and years of studies]. S (Study design): we included the following study designs- cross-sectional, longitudinal, and cohort studies published in English. The following studies were excluded: review articles, editorials, commentaries, letters to editors, case reports, studies without population denominators, studies conducted outside Nigeria, and studies with a small sample size of less than 50 [to minimize heterogeneity]. Operational definition Sickle cell disease was defined as an individual who inherited an abnormal hemoglobin S and another abnormal hemoglobin, which may include abnormal hemoglobin S, C, and S–beta-thalassemia [ 17 ]. Sickle cell anemia was defined as a condition in which an individual inherits two abnormal hemoglobin S (HbS) genes, resulting in a homozygous SS genotype, which is a type of sickle cell disease (SCD) [ 17 ]. Sickle cell trait was defined as an individual who inherited one normal hemoglobin A and one abnormal sickle cell gene hemoglobin, with resultant AS genotype [ 17 ]. Socioeconomic class was based on the methods described by Oyedeji, which were derived from the average of the highest educational attainment and occupational class, with cumulative scores sub-classified into upper, middle, and lower classes [ 18 ]. Study age groups ◦ Newborns: this referred to all neonates from day 0 to 28 of life [ 19 ]. ◦ Infants: this referred to children aged 12 months and below [ 20 ]. ◦ Under-fives: this referred to children below the age of 5 years [ 20 ]. ◦ Adolescents: this referred to adolescents aged 11 to 19 years [ 21 ]. ◦ All age groups: this referred to combinations of all ages, from day 0 of life to 19 years. Information sources and search The search used Medical Subject Headings [MeSH] terms, keywords, and entry words across the following databases: AJOL, Google Scholar, PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Scopus, and Web of Science. The search was conducted using the following words or phrases: “sickle cell disease OR sickle cell anemia OR sickle cell trait” AND “Nigeria” AND “newborns OR infants OR children OR adolescents” AND “associated factors OR sex OR socioeconomic status OR sociodemographic” AND “(SCD OR SCA OR SCT)” across the database (Supplementary Table S2). The search period included all studies published from January 1950 to October 2024. Selection process After searching, we exported all the search literature into the Rayyan software, where we removed duplicates. Two independent and blinded reviewers [AI and ORI] screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the eligible studies, which formed the basis for selecting studies for inclusion in this systematic review and meta-analysis. Where there was disagreement in the decision between the two reviewers, a third reviewer (MBA; a senior member of the research team) served as a tiebreaker. The authors of eligible studies with missing data were contacted via email and given adequate time to respond. Articles whose authors did not respond within a given timeframe were excluded. Data collection process We used the Rayyan systematic review screening tool and Microsoft Excel to extract the data. The extracted data included the first author’s name, year of publication, total number of study samples, number of events (SCD/SCT), location of study/geopolitical region, study design, study population (age groups), study settings (hospital or community-based study), sample size, sex, diagnostic method, and socioeconomic class. This review was reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) guidelines (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow charts of the study Study of risk of bias assessment and methodological quality assessment The risk of bias was minimized by allowing the principal investigator and co-investigator to perform different screening stages. The two reviewers were blinded to each other by using a screening tool. A third reviewer, acting as a tiebreaker, resolved the conflicts between the paired reviewers. A manual snowballing search for relevant studies was conducted by reviewing the references of selected studies and exploring the grey literature. We used the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale [NOS] adapted for cross-sectional studies to rate the quality of each included article [ 22 ]. In brief, the adapted tool consists of three domains: the first domain assesses the selection of the study participant with a graded maximum of five points; the second domain assesses comparability, including consideration of confounders, and has a maximum of two points; and the third domain addresses the outcomes and statistical tests with a maximum of three points. The NOS provides a cumulative maximum score of 10 points, which is further classified as high quality for scores of 7 and above, moderate quality for scores between 5 and 6, and low quality for scores below 5. Statistical analysis The extracted data [Microsoft Excel spreadsheet] was analyzed using MedCalc version 23 [statistical software package for biomedical research] and ‘Meta’ and ‘Metafor’ packages of R software (version 4.5.1), R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria. Due to anticipated heterogeneity, we used a random-effects model to measure the effect size of pooled prevalence, 95% confidence interval (CI) of SCD, and SCT. Similarly, random effect models were used to perform subgroup analysis of geopolitical regions, sex, age group, socioeconomic status, study methods, study settings, and diagnostic methods. We used forest plots to visually display each study’s prevalence estimates, their 95% confidence intervals, and the pooled summary estimates. Each forest plot also included weights for the common and random-effects models and predictive intervals [SCD and SCT]. To assess publication bias, we plotted the funnel plot of all included studies and further tested using Egger’s test for statistical significance. In addition, we carried out the ‘Trim-and-Fill’ to estimate the number of studies required to achieve symmetry of the funnel plot and re-calculated the pooled prevalence using the hypothetical studies. We performed I 2 , tau 2 (τ 2 ), and Q statistics on the pooled prevalence to assess the statistical heterogeneity. We considered I 2 values between 50 and 75%, and above 75% as moderate and high heterogeneity, respectively [ 23 ]. Sensitivity analyses using a leave-one-out approach were performed to examine the impact of each included study and the impact of outliers on the stability of the pooled prevalence of SCD and SCT. We applied a mixed-effects meta-regression model to explore the potential sources of heterogeneity in the pooled SCD prevalence. The moderators tested included years of studies, grouped into before 2000, 2001 to 2019, and 2020 to 2024; study setting (community-based vs. hospital-based—inpatients, outpatients, or both); age groups (newborns, infants, under-fives, adolescents, all ages); and methods of diagnosis (electrophoresis, high-performance liquid chromatography [HPLC], isoelectric focusing). Sex and socioeconomic classes were dropped from the meta-regression model because of missing data from the extracted studies. The model checked whether these factors significantly affected the differences in reported prevalence across studies, using an R 2 statistic to summarize the level of variation. The model coefficients, confidence intervals, and p-values were reported. For all levels of statistical significance, we set a p -value of < 0.05. Results Study selection We conducted a search between September and October 2024. The first search of the seven databases identified 26,815 articles. Another 10 articles were found by searching the references of the included articles and the grey literature, giving a cumulative total of 26,825 articles. These were screened step-by-step and reported using the PRISMA guidelines (Fig. 1 ). Finally, 30 articles that reported the prevalence of SCD and SCT were included in our review. Overview of included studies This review included 30 studies from all six geopolitical zones in Nigeria that met the inclusion criteria. The southwest had the highest representation, with seven articles (23.3%), while the southeast had six articles (20.0%); northwest (four studies, 13.3%), south-south (four studies, 13.3%), and north-central regions (five studies, 16.7%) (Table 1 ). Twenty-eight studies reported the prevalence of SCD with or without SCT, and twenty-one studies documented the prevalence of SCT. Four [13.3%] of the 30 studies were newborn screenings, two were conducted among infants [6.7%], and 19 [63.3%] included all age groups (Table 1 ). Twenty-seven [66.7%] of the studies were cross-sectional. Most studies were hospital-based [ n = 23, 76.7%], and five [16.7%] were community-based. The diagnostic methods included electrophoresis (12, 40.0%), high-performance liquid chromatography [6, 20.0%], isoelectric focusing (1, 3.3%), and 10 [33.3%] studies did not state the diagnostic methods (Table 1 ). Risk of bias assessment for the studies The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa scale adapted for cross-sectional studies to rate the quality of each included article [ 22 ]. All included studies, except one [moderate quality], were rated as high-quality studies (Table 1 ). The pooled prevalence of SCD and SCT among Nigerian children Using the random-effects model, the pooled prevalence of SCD in Nigeria was 4.0% [95% CI 3.0 to 6.0%]. However, the prevalence in the included studies ranged from 0.0 to 21.0% (Fig. 2 ) with significant heterogeneity ( I 2 = 99.6%, τ 2 = 0.0014). The pooled prevalence of SCT was 21.0% (95% CI 20.0 to 23.0%, I 2 = 90.5%,τ 2 = 0.0012), with significant heterogeneity (Fig. 3 ). There was no significant relationship between the various socioeconomic indices and SCD prevalence (Supplementary Fig. S7). The pooled community prevalence of SCD was 3.0% (95% CI 1.0 to 4.0%; I 2 = 87.3%, τ 2 = 0.0002) (Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. S8). Sensitivity analysis A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was conducted to examine the influence of individual studies on the pooled prevalence estimate. The results showed minimal changes in the pooled prevalence when each study was omitted in turn, with estimates ranging from 2.9% [Ibraheem et al. [ 47 ], Isezuo et al. [ 29 ]] to 3.2% [David et al. [ 33 ]], and overlapping confidence intervals between 2.1 and 4.7% (Supplementary Table S2 and Supplementary Fig. 11). This consistency indicates that no single study had an undue impact on the meta-analysis findings, thus supporting the overall robustness of the pooled prevalence estimate for SCD. Similarly, a leave-one-out sensitivity for SCT studies showed a stable pooled prevalence ranging from 21.1% [Idowu et al. [ 36 ]] to 22.1% [Amodu et al . [ 35 ]] with overlapping confidence between 19.5% and 23.3% (Supplementary Table S3 and Supplementary Fig. S12). These findings demonstrate that no single study exerted an undue influence on the pooled estimate, indicating the robustness and reliability of the meta-analysis. Heterogeneity and publication bias We applied a funnel plot and Egger’s test to assess publication bias. The funnel plot showed publication bias for studies included in the pooled prevalence of SCD (Fig. 4 ), which was confirmed by Egger’s test [intercept − 8.28, 95% CI − 14.15 to − 2.40, p = 0.008]. After applying the ‘Trim-and-Fill’ method, four studies were imputed to address potential funnel plot asymmetry. The adjusted pooled prevalence estimate was 4.0%, with a 95% CI of 2.7% to 5.9%, which remained similar to the original estimate of 4.0%. This finding suggests that publication bias is unlikely to substantially influence the overall findings (Supplementary Fig. S13). However, the heterogeneity persists with an I 2 of 99.5% with a large Q of 6270.23, suggesting significant heterogeneity among the studies. Therefore, while the trim-and-fill suggests the pooled prevalence is relatively robust, the considerable heterogeneity warrants cautious interpretation . In contrast, the studies included for SCT showed no considerable publication bias [Egger’s test-intercept − 0.409, 95% CI − 2.633 to 1.815, p = 0.795] (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 4 Funnel plots for publication bias assessment of studies included in the sickle cell disease pooled prevalence Fig. 5 Funnel plots for publication bias assessment of studies included in the sickle cell trait pooled prevalence Meta-regression The mixed-effects meta-regression (with multiple moderators) showed that studies conducted before 2000 reported significantly lower prevalence estimates than those conducted during 2000–2019 (estimate = − 0.816, p = 0.004). Similarly, studies classified as hospital-based (both outpatient and inpatient settings combined) had significantly lower prevalence estimates than community-based studies (estimate = − 1.0483, p = 0.010). Regarding diagnostic methods, studies that employed isoelectric focusing reported substantially lower prevalence estimates (estimate = − 2.8321, p < 0.001) than the reference diagnostic method [electrophoresis], while studies using HPLC showed a non-significant trend towards lower prevalence (estimate = − 0.8053, p = 0.120). Other variables, including the target age group categories, did not reach statistical significance, suggesting that the age distribution of the study population was not a significant source of heterogeneity in the reported prevalence (Supplementary Table S4). The overall model explained a substantial portion of the heterogeneity, with an estimated R 2 of 88.2%, indicating that the moderators collectively accounted for a large proportion of the observed between-study variability. The test of moderators was statistically significant (QM(df = 12) = 124.5, p < 0.0001), indicating that these covariates jointly explained the significant variability in SCD prevalence. Nonetheless, residual heterogeneity remained high ( I 2 = 93.2%), suggesting that other unmeasured factors may have contributed to differences among studies. Discussion Sickle cell disease (SCD) constitutes a significant public health burden in Nigeria, but its prevalence remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized data from 30 studies involving children and adolescents across all six geopolitical zones in Nigeria. This review provides pooled prevalence estimates for SCD and SCT, highlighting substantial variations across regions, age groups, diagnostic methods, study settings, and study designs. Pooled prevalence of SCD and SCT The pooled prevalence of SCD was 4.0%, which is higher than that reported in most individual studies in Nigeria. The prevalence across individual studies varied widely from 0.0 to 21.0%, with significant heterogeneity likely influenced by methodological differences, including study population, setting (hospital vs. community), design, and diagnostic methods used. Notably, the pooled prevalence of 4.0% exceeds the commonly cited 1–3% prevalence in Nigeria [ 24 , 49 ]. In addition, five studies reported a high prevalence of SCD (10–20.5%) [ 28 , 29 , 36 , 37 , 47 ], which was far above the pooled prevalence in this study. The higher rates were found by Ibraheem et al. [ 47 ], Isezuo et al. [ 29 ], and Yiltok et al. [ 28 ] could be because the studies were conducted in hospitals, which are more likely to have many SCD patients with different complications. In addition, the exceptionally high prevalence (21.0%) reported by Thanni et al. [ 37 ] could be due to a small sample size (78), resulting in an erroneously high prevalence value, which is difficult to generalize. Compared with global data, the pooled prevalence of SCD (4.0%) was substantially higher than the estimated 1.17% in a recent systematic review in India [ 7 ]. In addition, the pooled prevalence of 2.0% among under-fives far exceeded 0.11% from global estimates among similar age groups [ 50 ]. This prevalence is also higher than that reported in most sub-Saharan African countries—Kenya [ 5 ], the Democratic Republic of Congo [ 51 ], and Ghana [ 52 ]—further affirming the significant burden of SCD in Nigeria. A bit of concern was the sub-analysis of the years of the studies that shows a higher prevalence from 2001 compared with earlier years. While these findings are in keeping with a recent analysis of the ‘global burden of sickle cell disease’, the findings highlighted the need for the country to critically appraise the primary drivers of the rising burden of SCD in Nigeria and institute proactive measures to curb the rising trends [ 1 ]. The pooled prevalence of SCT was 21.0%, within the reported prevalence of 20–30% within the sub-Saharan region, consistent with earlier reports of a high carrier rate of the sickle cell gene in the country [ 53 ]. Although the sensitivity analysis showed that no single study had a major impact, it is important to note that studies by Idowu et al. [ 36 ] and Lema et al . [ 14 ] found very high prevalence rates of over 35%, likely because they had small sample sizes of 85 and 100, respectively. The high carrier prevalence observed in this study suggests the need for targeted interventions, such as premarital counseling, neonatal screening programs, and genetic counseling, to mitigate the burden of SCD in Nigeria. Furthermore, the SCT prevalence observed in this study falls within the reported prevalence in sub-Saharan Africa [10–40%] [ 3 ]. It is also three to four times higher than the pooled prevalence estimates in India [ 7 ] and other global reports [ 50 , 54 ], reflecting the influence of malaria-endemic regions where the sickle cell mutation confers a survival advantage. Genetic and sociocultural factors, such as consanguineous marriages in Nigerian-specific areas, may also contribute to these differences. The implication of one out of every five children and adolescents in this study having SCT demonstrated the need for proactive measures, such as premarital screening, as it remains a driver of SCD among the population. Regional variation in the prevalence of SCD/SCT across the geopolitical zones in Nigeria The highest pooled prevalence of SCD was recorded in the northwestern zone (7.0%), almost twice the national pooled prevalence and three and a half times higher than that in the southeastern zone (2.0%). These findings highlight regional disparities likely influenced by genetic, environmental, and healthcare-related factors. Concurrently, the northwest also had the highest pooled prevalence of SCT, partly explaining the higher SCD burden in the region. Sociocultural factors, such as consanguineous marriages, increase the likelihood of recessive genetic disorders and contribute to the observed regional differences [ 55 ]. Other factors, including awareness levels and access to diagnostic and treatment resources, may also play a significant role. Regional variations have also been documented in the Middle East [Saudi Arabia] [ 56 ], East Africa [Uganda] [ 56 ], and India [ 7 , 54 ], most of which are attributable to sociocultural practices similar to those in northern Nigeria. With country-limited resources, addressing these disparities requires region-specific public health intervention. Areas with a higher prevalence, such as the northwest, should be prioritized for genetic counseling, premarital screening, and neonatal screening initiatives. Conversely, regions with a lower prevalence, such as the southeast, should focus on sustaining and expanding healthcare services to maintain or reduce the disease burden. SCD prevalence based on gender, socioeconomic class, and study settings Five studies synthesized for the prevalence of SCD based on sex did not reveal differences in the burden in both males and females. This observation concurs with a systematic analysis of the “global burden of disease” on sickle cell disease [ 1 ] and a recent systematic review and meta-analysis in India [ 7 ]. Similarly, a population-based study of 735 rural school children from central India also showed no sex differences in the burden of SCD [ 57 ]. The observation of no sex differences among Nigerian children and adolescents is not unexpected, as the mode of inheritance of SCD is via the Mendelian pattern of autosomal recessive, which is not sex-linked [ 58 ]. The comparable burden in males and females demonstrated in this study suggests the need for Nigeria to strive to provide optimal care and support for all children and adolescents with sickle cell disease, irrespective of gender. We did not observe any relationship between the prevalence of SCD and socioeconomic status. This finding requires cautious interpretation because the synthesis included only two studies in the meta-analysis. While studies have demonstrated the impact of socioeconomic factors on SCD outcomes, only a few have explored the relationship between the prevalence of SCD and socioeconomic status [ 59 ]. On a comparative note, a study by Derman et al . [ 60 ] that included 1339 patients with SCD demonstrated a significant burden among those of low socioeconomic status. In contrast, a population-based study in central Gabon demonstrated no relationship between the prevalence of SCD and socioeconomic status [ 61 ]. Limited by two studies, there is a need to evaluate further the role of socioeconomic status among Nigerian children and adolescents regarding the prevalence of SCD. Future studies should include socioeconomic indices in SCD studies to ensure robust data analysis that could guide decisions in allocating available limited resources. This study also shows that the pooled prevalence of SCD is higher in the hospital-based studies than in the community-based studies. This finding is similar to a recent systematic review and analysis conducted in India [ 7 ]. The observations from this study that show a higher burden in hospital settings is expected because of selection bias, in which symptomatic children with SCD seek medical attention because of various complications. In contrast, community-based studies recruit broader, more representative, and larger population samples, usually with a large number of apparently healthy children. These findings imply the need to report the study settings, especially when the burden reported for SCD is higher than expected, and ensure proper interpretation. Confirming the significant burden in the hospital setting calls for a dedicated service for SCD with adequate support, especially at various Nigerian tertiary and secondary health facilities. This will ensure optimal care for the affected children and adolescents when they present at these health facilities. Quality of the studies, publication bias, and heterogeneity Overall, the quality of the included studies was rated as good, with 29 out of 30 rated as high quality, further supporting the reliability of our findings [ 22 ]. However, the significant findings of high heterogeneity are worth highlighting, indicating significant variations in the studies that are not explained by chance. This is not unexpected considering that more than two-thirds of the studies included were cross-sectional studies, which are more sensitive to contextual variation [ 62 ]. The high heterogeneity may reflect population characteristics (e.g., age, sex, region, and socioeconomic status), diagnostic criteria methods, study settings (hospital-based vs. community-based), and year of study. Despite the high heterogeneity observed in our analysis, the stability of the pooled prevalence after the ‘Trim-and-Fill’ of the funnels suggested the robustness of our findings and accurate reflections of the burden of SCD in Nigeria. Indeed, the consistency of the pooled estimates when each study was omitted demonstrates that the meta-analysis results are robust and enhance confidence in the pooled results’ validity for both SCD and SCT studies. To further address the high heterogeneity, we applied a meta-regression model, which revealed that a substantial proportion of this heterogeneity ( R 2 = 88%) was attributable to the year of study, diagnostic methods, and study settings. This finding is not unexpected given the population dynamics over the study period, the accuracy of various diagnostic methods, and the potential selection bias related to the study settings. Implications for public health policy, clinical, and research implications Public health policy The high burden of SCD, which is as high as 7% in northwestern Nigeria, indicates the need for the urgent implementation of universal screening of newborns in the country. Universal screening has been demonstrated to be feasible in Nigeria and will ensure the early enrollment of confirmed cases and close monitoring to mitigate poor outcomes [ 26 ]. The regional variation from this study also demonstrates the need to prioritize northwestern and southwestern Nigeria, where a significant burden of SCD exists regarding public health intervention, including universal newborn screening, community education, awareness campaigns on SCD and SCT, treatment, and other supportive care. Notwithstanding, health awareness campaigns across geopolitical zones and appropriate legislation to determine genotypes among intending couples will also be crucial for the nation to stem rising SCD trends. Clinical practice implications The findings of this study show a significant burden of SCD among hospital-based studies and suggest the need to strengthen and improve access for children and adolescents with SCD [ 63 ]. Healthcare workers also need a high index of suspicion to allow prompt early diagnosis and referral to specialized centers for SCD for optimal care and improve outcome. The SCD centers across the six geopolitical zones in Nigeria should ensure that care is extended beyond the vicinity of their facilities [ 9 ]. This will ensure sick children and adolescents with SCD will have improved access to quality care, affordable, and ultimately improved outcomes. Research implications While the burden of SCT appears stable, the higher prevalence of SCD highlights the need to explore the drivers of SCD in Nigeria. Exploring the drivers of SCD in Nigeria would allow for targeted interventions in preventive measures and ultimately reduce the burden on the country. Most of the studies in this study are cross-sectional and suggest the need for cohort and longitudinal studies to measure the impact of SCD on Nigerian children and adolescents. The limited data on socioeconomics also suggests the need to carry out more studies on the roles of socioeconomic class in the study, as we are careful not to make a definitive conclusion on a pooled analysis with two datasets. Future research The significant burden of SCD with regional variations demonstrated in this study suggests the need for the country to urgently understudy the main drivers of the burden of SCD and design appropriate interventions in the short- and long-term with goals and timelines to reduce its burden. This will ensure that, while care is being offered to those with the disease, the burden is progressively reduced with a reduction in the number of new cases, ultimately improving the country's SCD/SCT indices. Study limitations Some studies reported extreme prevalence values of 0.0% for SCD, which could have resulted from small sample sizes, misclassifications, or limitations in diagnostic accuracy [ 10 , 33 , 42 ]. A few sub-analyses, such as socioeconomic class, have only two studies that could have affected the outcomes. In addition, the language search for this study was limited to English, with the possibility of missing studies published in other languages. However, we expect this to be minimal, if any, because Nigeria’s official language is English. In addition, we could not carry out a subgroup analysis [rural vs. urban], which would have allowed us to further explore other sources of heterogeneity owing to the non-availability of such data from the source literature. Another limitation of our studies is the inclusion of studies with diagnostic methods that are not clearly stated. These studies were included because they emanated from tertiary centers and were retrospective, with data retrieved from the archives of the SCD database. Conclusion This review underscores the significant burden of SCD in Nigeria, which has a higher-than-expected prevalence and the highest burden occurring in the northwestern geopolitical zone in Nigeria. In addition, there was no relationship between sex, socioeconomic class, and prevalence of SCD. These findings emphasize the need for region-specific, culturally sensitive interventions to mitigate the impact of the disease. Additionally, the significant differences between studies highlight the need for consistent diagnostic procedures and a national hemoglobinopathy registry to help accurately track the disease and guide policy choices. Addressing these gaps would improve SCD management and reduce the public health burden in Nigeria. documents.title: Chikungunya seroprevalence in the Horn of Africa: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) poses a significant burden on affected populations, presenting substantial challenges to public health. This study aimed to assess the seroprevalence of the CHIKV in the Horn of Africa.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis by searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Scientific Direct, Google Scholar, and reference lists for primary articles published from the inception of the database until November 30, 2023. The inclusion criteria covered seroprevalence studies of CHIKV in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Eritrea, Uganda, and Djibouti. Pooled seroprevalence was estimated using a random effects model, and the meta-analysis was conducted with R Studio version 4.3.1 and the Metapro package. The study protocol adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and is registered in PROSPERO, CRD42023477057.
RESULTS: From a pool of 87,567 potential studies, 34 eligible studies were included in our analysis. Most of the studies were conducted in Kenya (44%). Hospital-based studies were included in 59% of cases. A total of 23,400 participants were involved in the review. Of the 13,397 participants, 6778 (67.6% of those with information) were male. The pooled seroprevalence of CHIKV was 14% (95% CI: 9-23; I2 = 99%). Subgroup analysis was performed. The seroprevalence was higher in studies conducted in population settings: 15% (95% CI: 5-37; I2 = 99%) than in hospital settings. The seroprevalence of chikungunya was high from the 2004 to 2013 period, at 36% (95% CI: 13-68; I2 = 98%). Plaque reduction neutralization tests detected 15% (95% CI: 3-49%; I2 = 94%) of the chikungunya seroprevalence. The seroprevalence of CHIKV among inapparent infections was 17% (95% CI: 8-35; I2 = 98%). The meta-regression analysis revealed that the chikungunya seroprevalence was predicted by the countries of study, age group, and trends of infection over time.
CONCLUSION: Our review highlights compelling evidence of CHIKV and other arbovirus circulation in the Horn of Africa, revealing diverse seroprevalence rates across different countries, age groups, laboratory tests, clinical manifestations, and time trends. The confirmatory gold standard, the plaque reduction neutralization test, increases diagnostic accuracy.

Introduction Chikungunya is a mosquito-borne viral disease caused by chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a RNA virus in the alphavirus genus of the family Togaviridae. [ 1 ] It is transmitted to humans through the bite of female Aedes spp. mosquitoes (mostly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus ). The virus was identified in 1952 in the Newala district of Tanzania, where it was named from the language of the Makonde people, meaning “bends up,” pointing to severe joint pain. [ 2 ] Since then, the virus has evolved into 4 major genotypes, the East-Central-South-African and West African genotypes, which are associated with epidemics in the sub-Saharan regions, and the Asian genotype and the Indian Ocean lineage, which are linked with epidemics in parts of Asia and the Indian Ocean islands. [ 3 ] Chikungunya symptoms include fever, headache, rash, fatigue, myalgia, and severe polyarthralgia. [ 4 ] The incubation period ranged from 1 to 12 days. [ 5 ] While the acute symptoms generally last from a few days to 2 weeks, the debilitating polyarthralgia can persist for months or even years in a significant proportion of patients, leading to chronic morbidity. [ 6 ] Notably, certain individuals, particularly those of advanced age or with comorbid conditions, may experience an atypical presentation of the disease. [ 6 , 7 ] This atypical form can include severe neurological, dermal, or cardiovascular complications, and even mortality, diverging from the classic symptomatology. The clinical presentation of CHIKV infection shares significant overlap with other arboviruses. Dengue fever is more common in the tropics and subtropics. It commonly presents with a high fever, headache, body aches, nausea, and rash. [ 8 , 9 ] Most patients will also improve within 1 to 2 weeks and have an asymptomatic presentation. Zika virus generally has mild symptoms, including rash, fever, conjunctivitis, muscle and joint pain, malaise, and headache, and usually lasts for 2 to 7 days. [ 10 ] Another common arbovirus is yellow fever. Symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite. [ 11 , 12 ] In most cases, symptoms disappear after 3 to 4 days. O’nyong-nyong virus (ONNV) is clinically associated with fever, polyarthralgia, rash, and lymph node involvement. [ 13 ] Unlike other arboviruses such as chikungunya, dengue fever, Zika, and yellow fever, it is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and tends to occur in areas where malaria is also common. [ 14 ] It is genetically and antigenically closely related to CHIKV. [ 15 , 16 ] Adding to the diagnostic challenge is the possibility of co-infections with multiple arboviruses circulating in the same region. These clinical similarities and the potential for co-infections make diagnosis very difficult. The diagnostic modalities used for chikungunya are serologic and molecular tests. [ 17 ] Serologic testing includes viral antigen–antibody detection, which is achieved by using an immunoglobulin M (IgM)/immunoglobulin G (IgG) enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), an immunofluorescence assay (IFA), hemagglutination inhibition test (HI), a rapid diagnostic test, and immunoblotting methods. They are used in the acute phase and have different sensitivities and specificities. In addition, these tests are easier to perform, cost-effective, and require minimal resources than molecular tests. [ 18 ] However, because of the cross-reactivity of recombinant CHIKV E1 and E2-encoded proteins with the ONNV, confirmatory tests such as plaque reduction neutralization tests (PRNTs) are needed. [ 19 ] Moreover, molecular techniques such as reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and isothermal amplification remain the gold standards for diagnostic tests. [ 20 ] Several factors facilitate the spread of CHIKV such as population density, human migration, urbanization, lack of immunity, and vector adaptations, inadequate vector control programs further contribute to outbreak potential. [ 21 – 23 ] In addition, studies have shown that the incidence of chikungunya varies with factors such as occupation, age, sex, education, and outdoor activities. [ 24 ] Farmers and older people are associated with higher prevalence rates. [ 25 ] CHIKV outbreaks have been reported globally, with a significant burden in Africa. The continent has experienced numerous epidemics, and in the context of increasing globalization and human migration, these outbreaks have frequently spread beyond their initial foci. [ 26 , 27 ] The 1st case of CHIKV in Ethiopia was identified in the Dollo Ado district, Somali region of Ethiopia, in June 2016, and it was imported from the border of Mandera County, Kenya. [ 28 ] Subsequently, outbreak cases were reported in the Dire Dawa city administration, the Ad’ar district of the Afar region, the Somali region, and the Dawro zone. [ 29 – 32 ] In 2004, Kenya experienced an outbreak. [ 33 ] Sudan [ 34 – 36 ] and Djibouti [ 37 ] have also experienced outbreaks. The potential for disease outbreaks, co-infections with other arboviruses, severe and atypical forms, as well as the lack of vaccines and difficulty in controlling the disease, highlight the importance of scientific knowledge regarding the true burden of chikungunya. As a result, the objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to assess CHIKV seroprevalence and highlight its coinfections with other arboviruses in the Horn of Africa. The aim of measuring CHIKV seroprevalence in the region is to help public health officials understand virus propagation, identify high-risk locations, and improve disease control and prevention initiatives between nations across borders. 2. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted, and the report followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. [ 38 ] The protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO, CRD42023477057. 2.1. Eligibility criteria The condition, context, and population (CoCoPop) description model was used to set eligibility criteria for the study. Condition: CHIKV seroprevalence in populations is determined by laboratory diagnosis of prior or current infection by antibody detection methods such as ELISA using IgG and IgM, IFA, and HI. Studies that included outbreaks and used RT-PCR tests only were excluded from the review. Context: reported seroprevalence studies of CHIKV in the Horn of Africa which includes Ethiopia, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Eritrea, Djibouti, and Uganda, were included. Populations: the review covered all studies done across all age groups. Study design: observational studies, such as case–control, cross-sectional, and cohort studies, were included in the review. Review articles, editorials, commentaries, conference abstracts and studies for which the full text is not available were excluded. In addition to this studies not published in English language were excluded. 2.2. Search strategy A systematic literature search was performed to identify relevant articles from the online databases. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Science Direct, and Google Scholar, and other reference lists were searched for primary articles published from the inception of the database until November 30, 2023. The search was performed in accordance with the recommendations in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. [ 39 ] The search strategies used in PubMed for the text words were as follows: (((((“chikungunya virus”[MeSH Terms] OR (“chikungunya”[All Fields] AND “virus”[All Fields]) OR “chikungunya virus”[All Fields] OR (“chikungunya fever”[MeSH Terms] OR (“chikungunya”[All Fields] AND “fever”[All Fields]) OR “chikungunya fever”[All Fields])) AND (“seroepidemiologic studies”[MeSH Terms] OR (“seroepidemiologic”[All Fields] AND “studies”[All Fields]) OR “seroepidemiologic studies”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalence”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalences”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalance”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalances”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalency”[All Fields] OR “seroprevalent”[All Fields])) OR “Seroepidemiology”[All Fields]) AND (“ethiopia”[MeSH Terms] OR “ethiopia”[All Fields] OR “ethiopia s”[All Fields])) OR (“somalia”[MeSH Terms] OR “somalia”[All Fields] OR “somalia s”[All Fields]) OR (“sudan”[MeSH Terms] OR “sudan”[All Fields] OR “sudans”[All Fields] OR “sudan s”[All Fields]) OR (“south sudan”[MeSH Terms] OR (“south”[All Fields] AND “sudan”[All Fields]) OR “south sudan”[All Fields]) OR (“kenya”[MeSH Terms] OR “kenya”[All Fields] OR “kenya s”[All Fields]) OR (“eritrea”[MeSH Terms] OR “eritrea”[All Fields]) OR (“djibouti”[MeSH Terms] OR “djibouti”[All Fields]) OR (“uganda”[MeSH Terms] OR “uganda”[All Fields] OR “uganda s”[All Fields])). 2.3. Study selection We used the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 39 ] and R Studio version 4.3.1 Metapro package for data management and analysis. Two authors (YA and DGA) independently reviewed the results, and disagreements were resolved through discussion. 2.4. Data extraction and management The title and abstract were retrieved from the electronic search and reference lists and independently screened by 2 authors. Data were extracted from each included study using a standardized form, including information on the author, journal and year of publication, country and city, period, study design, study population, age, sex, laboratory test, clinical symptoms, number of positive results (event), and total sample size. 2.5. Risk of bias assessment The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality checklist for a cross-sectional study design was used to assess the risk of bias (ROB). [ 40 , 41 ] If the quality of the study fulfilled the methodological requirement, 1 score was assigned to each item. A score of 0 to 4 indicates a high ROB, 5 to 7 indicates a moderate ROB, and 8 to 11 indicates a low ROB. Two reviewers (YA and MSK) performed the assessments separately, and discrepancies were resolved through discussions with a third reviewer (TM). 2.6. Data synthesis The pooled seroprevalence of CHIKV in the study population was calculated using meta-analysis methods, including a random effects model, to account for heterogeneity between studies. 2.7. Assessment of heterogeneity Forest plots were constructed to assess heterogeneity among the included studies. The Cochrane Q and I 2 statistics, which measure the percentage of variance resulting from true differences in the effect sizes rather than the sampling error, were used to measure heterogeneity among the studies. [ 42 ] We performed subgroup analyses according to the key potential sources of heterogeneity among the countries of study, study settings, laboratory diagnostic tests used, 3 age groups, trends of infection over time and clinical manifestations. Furthermore, given the high degree of heterogeneity of the true differences in the effect sizes, we ran a meta-regression to regress the prevalence. A funnel plot and Egger regression test were used to assess publication bias in the studies. [ 43 ] To determine statistical significance, the Chi 2 test with a P value of <.05 was used. 3. Results The search resulted in a total of 87,567 studies, of which 54 full-text eligible studies were evaluated further; 34 [ 33 , 44 – 76 ] of these studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis and qualitative analysis (Fig. 1 ). Figure 1. PRISMA flow diagram illustrating the study selection process for the systematic review and meta-analysis of chikungunya virus seroprevalence in the Horn of Africa. PRISMA = Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. 3.1. Study characteristics Total of 23,400 participant involved in the review. Most of the studies were conducted in Kenya (44%), [ 33 , 54 , 55 , 57 – 62 , 64 , 67 , 68 , 73 – 75 ] Sudan (23.5%), [ 45 , 46 , 52 , 65 , 67 , 69 , 72 , 76 ] Uganda (14.7%), [ 49 , 50 , 56 , 63 , 70 ] and Ethiopia (8.8%). [ 47 , 51 , 53 ] Fifty-nine percent of the studies were hospital-based, [ 33 , 45 , 46 , 49 – 51 , 53 , 56 – 58 , 60 , 62 , 63 , 65 – 67 , 69 , 70 , 75 , 76 ] and 38% of the studies were population based. [ 33 , 44 , 47 , 48 , 52 , 54 , 55 , 59 , 61 , 64 , 68 , 73 , 74 ] Of the 13,397 participants, 6778 (67.6% of those with information) were male. Seventy-three percent of the studies were performed among all age groups, while 15% and 12% of the studies were performed among children (<18 years) and adults (>18 years), respectively. Out of 34 studies, 43% were conducted in participants with inapparent infections [ 44 , 47 , 50 – 52 , 54 , 57 , 61 , 64 , 66 , 68 , 70 – 73 ] and 43% in symptomatic infections, [ 44 , 46 , 47 , 51 , 56 – 58 , 60 , 61 , 63 , 65 , 69 , 74 , 75 ] whereas 14% of studies [ 33 , 55 , 56 , 69 , 74 ] did not clearly state the clinical symptoms information in the primary studies. ELISA was only performed for 65% of the studies. Of these, 54.5% were IgG and 41% were IgM/IgG. Only the hemagglutination test was performed for 23.5% of the studies. Moreover, a PRNT was performed for 44% of the studies. Among those coinfected with arboviruses, 32% were infected with dengue virus, [ 44 , 45 , 49 , 50 , 55 , 57 , 59 , 64 , 68 , 70 , 73 ] 38% with yellow fever, [ 44 , 47 – 51 , 54 , 56 , 57 , 64 , 70 , 72 , 73 ] 11.7% with Zika virus, [ 47 – 49 , 54 ] 11.7% with Rift Valley virus, [ 44 , 48 , 64 , 68 ] and 17.6% with West Nile virus. [ 48 – 50 , 54 , 57 , 72 ] Malaria coinfection occurred in 1 study. [ 59 ] The review revealed that the common reasons for the high chikungunya seroprevalence in the Horn of Africa were household density, large family size, sleeping in open at night, travel history to forest, favorable breeding sites for vectors, climate and environmental fluctuations, farming/irrigation, long rainy seasons and frequent outbreaks in the region. Risk of bias in studies Overall, the risk of bias was low in 20%, moderate in 65.7%, and high in 14.3% of the studies. The risk of bias assessments are summarized in Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content, https://links.lww.com/MD/R324 . 3.3. Pooled seroprevalence of CHIKV The overall seroprevalence of CHIKV identified in the 34 studies was 14% (95% CI: 9–23; I 2 = 99%), participants = 23,400 (Fig. 2 ). Figure 2. Forest plot of the overall pooled seroprevalence of chikungunya virus in the Horn of Africa. 3.4. Subgroup analysis 3.4.1. The seroprevalence of CHIKV among countries The seroprevalence of CHIKV in Ethiopia was 27% (95% CI: 8–61; I 2 = 96%), followed by Kenya at 18% (95% CI: 9–33; I 2 = 99%), Uganda at 17% (95% CI: 3–55; I 2 = 99%), and Sudan at 14% (95% CI: 4–40; I 2 = 96%), as shown in Figure 3 . Figure 3. Forest plot of the subgroup analysis of chikungunya virus seroprevalence by country. 3.4.2. The seroprevalence of CHIKV among the study population The seroprevalence was higher in study conducted in population settings 15% (95% CI: 5–37; I 2 = 99%) than in those conducted in hospital settings 12% (95% CI: 7–21; I 2 = 98%), as shown in Figure 4 . Figure 4. Forest plot of the subgroup analysis of chikungunya virus seroprevalence by study setting (population based vs hospital-based). 3.4.3. The seroprevalence of CHIKV among age groups The seroprevalence of CHIKV was higher among adults 40% (95% CI: 13–74; I 2 = 96%) than other age groups, as shown in Figure 5 . Figure 5. Forest plot of the subgroup analysis of chikungunya virus seroprevalence by age group. 3.4.4. The seroprevalence of CHIKV based on diagnostic tests The seroprevalence of CHIKV was higher in studies that used ELISA 14% (95% CI: 7–25; I 2 = 99%), followed by the HI test 11% (95% CI: 3–34; I 2 = 90%) as shown in Figure 6 . Among the ELISA tests performed, the seroprevalence of chikungunya using IgG was 11% (95% CI: 6–20; I 2 = 99%), followed by IgM at 4% (95% CI: 2–12; I 2 = 93%), as shown in Figures 7 and 8 . The seroprevalence of chikungunya in the Horn of Africa among those studies that used the gold standard confirmatory test, PRNT, was 15% (95% CI: 3–49%; I 2 = 94%), as shown in Figure 9 . Out of which, 24% of the PRNTs cross-reacted with ONNV only, and 36% of the PRNTs cross-reacted with both CHIKV and ONNV. Figure 6. The trend of CHIKV seroprevalence over a period of time The seroprevalence of CHIKV was 11% (95% CI: 4–31; I 2 = 90%), 36% (95% CI: 13–68; I 2 = 98%) and 11% (95% CI: 5–21; I 2 = 99%) between 1954 and 2004, 2004 and 2013, and 2014 and 2023, respectively, as shown in Figure 11 . Figure 11. Forest plot of the subgroup analysis of chikungunya virus seroprevalence over time (1954–2004, 2004–2013, 2014–2023). 3.5. Meta-regression analysis To better explain the heterogeneity of the chikungunya seroprevalence in the Horn of Africa, a meta-regression analysis that considered several factors at the same time was performed. The meta-regression results revealed that the seroprevalence of CHIKV was highest in Ethiopia 2.8 (95% CI: 0.82–4.8; P value: .008), followed by Kenya 2.52 (95% CI: 0.83–4.21; P value: .0056) and Sudan 1.92 (95% CI: 0.07–3.78), P value = .042. The chikungunya seroprevalence in children was −2.46 (95% CI: −4.43 to −0.49), P value = .017 and that in all age groups was −1.68 (95% CI −3.12 to −0.25), P value = .023, which was significantly lower than that in adults. The chikungunya seroprevalence rate between 2004 and 2013 was 1.35 (95% CI: 0.18–2.53), and the P value was .025, which was higher than that in other periods, as shown in Table 2 .
